docs.title: Flan: Turbulent Trace Impurity Transport
docs.text:
Flan follows trace amounts of impurities through turbulent plasmas. It's a Monte Carlo code that tracks each impurity ion's full gyro-orbit through a time-dependent background plasma, usually a turbulence simulation from Gkeyll, and records where the impurities go. The result is the impurity density, flow and charge state throughout the plasma, as they evolve in time with the turbulence.

Tungsten density from a Flan simulation of the DIII-D far-SOL during shot #167196, 64 µs into the run.

docs.title: What Flan does
docs.text:
Impurities, i.e., atoms other than the main plasma species, enter a fusion plasma from the walls and other plasma-facing components. Even in small amounts they can radiate away power and dilute the fuel, so where they go is important. In the scrape-off layer (SOL), the transport is dominated by turbulence, which existing impurity transport codes typically model with simple diffusion and pinch coefficients.

Flan instead follows the impurities through the turbulence itself. For a heavy impurity like tungsten, the gyroradius is comparable to the size of the turbulent fluctuations, so the usual guiding-center approximation breaks down. Flan makes no such approximation: every particle is pushed through the electric and magnetic fields with its full gyromotion resolved.

Flan is a trace impurity code. The impurities are assumed to be too few to change the background plasma, and they don't interact with each other. Each one is followed independently through the background, which is what lets the calculation be spread across many CPU cores, nodes and GPUs.

docs.title: What it can simulate
docs.text:
• Impurity transport in turbulent plasmas. The main use is impurities in the SOL of a tokamak, in a time-dependent turbulent background from a Gkeyll simulation, e.g., tungsten in the DIII-D far-SOL. Flan works with Gkeyll's field-aligned, curvilinear coordinates.
  • Many impurity species. Any impurity can be followed. With ionization/recombination on, OpenADAS data is used for H through Ne, Al, Si, Cl, Ar, Fe, Kr, Mo, Xe and W.
  • Where impurities start. Particles can start at one location and time, over a range, or anywhere in the simulation, with a set temperature or the local ion temperature, and in any charge state, including as neutrals.
  • Different boundaries. Each boundary can absorb particles, wrap them around (periodic), or send them back in from a random spot along it, as for particles entering the core.
  • Textbook test cases. Built-in test backgrounds check that Flan reproduces gyration, the ExB, grad-B, polarization and curvature drifts, and the friction force from the collision model.

The output is a netCDF file with the impurity density, the average velocity (in both Cartesian and the simulation's coordinates), the average charge state and more, on the background's grid at every time frame.

docs.title: Physics
docs.text:
• Full-orbit particle push with the energy-conserving Boris algorithm. The fields are interpolated in space and time to each particle's position. See Impurity Transport.
  • Coulomb collisions with the background ions and electrons, using the Nanbu model, which is valid for any collisionality. See Collisions.
  • Ionization and recombination from OpenADAS rate coefficients. See Ionization/Recombination.

docs.title: Performance
docs.text:
Flan is written in C++ and built for large simulations, up to hundreds of millions of particles:

  • OpenMP threads on each node, see OpenMP Layout.
  • MPI across nodes, see MPI Parallelism.
  • NVIDIA GPUs with CUDA, with the same physics as the CPU version. One build runs on either, chosen when the simulation starts.

docs.title: Getting started
docs.text:
1. Install Flan on your machine, as a CPU or GPU build.
  2. Set up and run a case. The ExB drift test there is a good first run.
  3. Choose your input options.

docs.title: Input Options
docs.text:
Input options are set in your input file through the inpts map, e.g.:

inpts["case_name"] = "my_case";
inpts["imp_num"] = 10000;
inpts["imp_mass_amu"] = 183.84;

Any option you don't set uses the default value listed below. The options are grouped by what they control.

Mistakes in options stop the run

Flan stops with an error before the simulation starts if an option name isn't recognized (e.g., a typo), a value has the wrong type, or a string option has a value that isn't one of its valid values. The type must match the table exactly. For example, inpts["imp_num"] = 1e4 is a double, so use inpts["imp_num"] = 10000 for an int option.

docs.title: Simulation
docs.text: Option Type Default Description case_name string "undefined" Name of the simulation case. The results are saved to <case_name>.nc. use_gpu string "off" Whether to run the simulation on GPUs. Valid values: "off", "cuda". seed int -1 Base seed for the random number generators. A negative value (the default) seeds them from the clock so each run is different. Set it to 0 or above to make a run repeatable. The MPI rank is added to the seed so each rank gets a different sequence. slot_cap int 1048576 Maximum number of particle slots, i.e., the most particles followed at once. The number of slots used is the smaller of this and imp_num. print_interval int 10 Number of progress updates printed while particles are followed. For example, 10 prints an update every 10% of particles.

docs.title: Background plasma
docs.text: Option Type Default Description bkg_source string "gkeyll" Source of the background plasma, either a built-in test background or a Gkeyll simulation. Valid values: "test", "gkeyll". min_ne float 1e15 Lower limit on the electron density (m^-3). min_te float 0.1 Lower limit on the electron temperature (eV). min_ti float 0.1 Lower limit on the ion temperature (eV), applied when calculating collisions with the background ions and when sampling starting velocities with imp_temp_start_opt = "main_ion".

docs.title: Testing
docs.text: Option Type Default Description test_opt string "gyrate" Which built-in test case to run when using the test background. Valid values: "gyrate", "exb", "gradb", "polarization", "curvature", "friction_force". save_track string "off" Whether to save particle tracks to the output file. Valid values: "off", "on".

docs.title: Gkeyll
docs.text: Option Type Default Description gkyl_dir string "undefined" Directory containing the Gkeyll simulation files. gkyl_casename string "undefined" Name of the Gkeyll case, i.e., the prefix of its output files. gkyl_frame_start int 0 First Gkeyll frame to load. gkyl_frame_end int 1 Last Gkeyll frame to load. The range from gkyl_frame_start to gkyl_frame_end is inclusive. gkyl_elec_name string "elc" Name of the electron species in the Gkeyll simulation. gkyl_ion_name string "ion" Name of the main ion species in the Gkeyll simulation. gkyl_elec_mass_amu float 0.000548 Electron mass used in the Gkeyll simulation (amu). gkyl_ion_mass_amu float 2.014 Main ion mass used in the Gkeyll simulation (amu). gkyl_file_type string "binary" File format of the Gkeyll output. Valid values: "binary". gkyl_moment_type string "bimaxwellian" Type of moment files in the Gkeyll output. Collisions need "bimaxwellian", which provides the ion parallel flow and perpendicular velocity used to calculate the background flow. Valid values: "bimaxwellian", "maxwellian", "m0m1m2". calc_grad_elec string "off" Whether to calculate the electric field gradient. This is not implemented yet, so turning it on only prints a warning. Valid values: "off", "on".

docs.title: Geometry and boundaries
docs.text:
Option Type Default Description tbound_type string "absorbing" Boundary condition at the start and end of the background time range. Valid values: "absorbing", "periodic". min_xbound_type string "absorbing" Boundary condition at the minimum x boundary. Valid values: "absorbing", "periodic", "core". max_xbound_type string "absorbing" Boundary condition at the maximum x boundary. Valid values: "absorbing", "periodic", "core". min_ybound_type string "absorbing" Boundary condition at the minimum y boundary. Valid values: "absorbing", "periodic", "core". max_ybound_type string "absorbing" Boundary condition at the maximum y boundary. Valid values: "absorbing", "periodic", "core". min_zbound_type string "absorbing" Boundary condition at the minimum z boundary. Valid values: "absorbing", "periodic", "core". max_zbound_type string "absorbing" Boundary condition at the maximum z boundary. Valid values: "absorbing", "periodic", "core". lcfs_x float 0.0 x coordinate of the last closed flux surface. lcfs_y float 0.0 y coordinate of the last closed flux surface. lcfs_z float 0.0 z coordinate of the last closed flux surface. imp_xbound_buffer float 0.0 Buffer distance at the x boundaries. With an absorbing boundary, a particle is absorbed once it is within this distance of the boundary. imp_ybound_buffer float 0.0 Buffer distance at the y boundaries. With an absorbing boundary, a particle is absorbed once it is within this distance of the boundary. imp_zbound_buffer float 0.0 Buffer distance at the z boundaries. With an absorbing boundary, a particle is absorbed once it is within this distance of the boundary. sep_x_bc_xp_z1 float 0.0 First z value for the separatrix x boundary condition near the X-point. sep_x_bc_xp_z2 float 0.0 Second z value for the separatrix x boundary condition near the X-point.

Periodic boundaries must be periodic on both sides

A periodic boundary wraps a particle around to the other side of the domain, so it only makes sense if both the minimum and maximum boundaries in that direction are periodic. If only one side of x, y or z is set to "periodic", Flan prints a warning and sets both sides to "periodic".

docs.title: Journal Articles
docs.text:
• S. A. Zamperini, T. N. Bernard, S. Andersen, A. C. D. Hoffmann, D. L. Rudakov, and T. Abrams, "Fully generalized, turbulent trace impurity transport with Gkeyll and Flan in the DIII-D far-SOL," Plasma Physics and Controlled Fusion 68, 075013 (2026). doi:10.1088/1361-6587/ae836b

    The first official Flan publication. Validation tests are shown, and tungsten transport in the DIII-D far-SOL is simulated. Main takeaways are an early attempt at extracting the anomalous diffusion and pinch velocities as well as the observation that transport away from the wall increases with atomic number.

  • S. A. Zamperini, T. N. Bernard, D. L. Rudakov, and J. A. Boedo, "Turbulent drifts of impurity ions as an explanation for anomalous radial transport in the far-SOL of DIII-D," Nuclear Fusion 64, 074002 (2024). doi:10.1088/1741-4326/ad4c78

    A python-based precursor to Flan that tracked impurities via their guiding centers. It became clear that the guiding center approximation was violated because the fluctuations were on the same scale as the tungsten gyroradius, and that the full gyro-orbit needed to be resolved. This was the key issue that showed the need for a proper high-performance code that resolved the gyro-orbit and all the additional Monte Carlo structure.

docs.title: Code Structure
docs.text: Flan is a C++ library, libflan.so. A simulation is a small C++ program, the input file, that fills in an Inputs map of options and calls flan(). Everything else happens inside the library. This page describes how the library is organized, how a run flows through it, and how the CPU and GPU versions of the code fit together. The API Reference has the documentation for every function, generated from the comments in the source code.

docs.title: Repository layout
docs.text:
Directory Contents src/ The library source. One .cpp file per part of the code (options, background, Boris push, collisions, ...). src/cuda/ The GPU (CUDA) versions of the main loop steps, plus the code that copies data to and from the GPU. Only built with CUDA enabled. include/ Headers for src/. include/cuda/ Headers for src/cuda/, and the small inline helpers used inside kernels (interpolation, indexing, ...). tests/ Unit tests (GoogleTest), run with ctest. regression/ Input files for the test cases (drifts, friction force) and a blank input file to start from. python/ Helper scripts: reading Gkeyll data with postgkyl (read_gkyl.py), generating the Nanbu table (calc_nanbu_A.py) and plotting (flan_plots.py). scripts/ Case setup (flan_setup.sh) and job submission scripts. docs-site/ This website.

src/tmp/ and include/tmp/ hold old code kept for reference. They aren't built.

docs.title: How a run works
docs.text:
An input file looks like this (see regression/blank_input_file.cpp):

int main(int argc, char* argv[])
{
    MPI_Init(&argc, &argv);
    Inputs inpts {create_inputs()};  // Fill in the options
    flan(inpts);
    MPI_Finalize();
}

MPI must be initialized before flan() is called, and every rank calls it. flan() (src/flan.cpp) then runs the simulation in five steps:

  1. Load the options. Options::load_options starts from the defaults and overwrites them with the values in inpts. An unrecognized option name, a value of the wrong type or an invalid value stops the run.
  2. Read the background. Background::read_bkg loads the plasma on rank 0, from a Gkeyll simulation (Gkyl::read_gkyl) or one of the built-in test backgrounds (Test::read_test). It's then broadcast to every rank.
  3. Follow the impurities. ImpurityTransport::follow_impurities follows this rank's share of the particles and records their statistics.
  4. Combine the statistics. Impurity::reduce_stats adds up the statistics from every rank on rank 0, which then calculates the density, average velocities, average charge and average Nanbu s from them.
  5. Save the results. SaveResults::save_results writes everything to <case_name>.nc on rank 0, and the timing summary is printed.

docs.title: The main loop
docs.text:
follow_impurities sets up the particle slots, the OpenADAS rate coefficients and the random number generators, copies everything to the GPUs if they're on, and then runs main_loop (src/impurity_transport.cpp). Before the loop starts, the slots are filled, the starting cells are found and the velocities are pushed back half a time step for the leapfrog scheme. Then each pass through the loop runs these steps, in order:

Step Wrapper CPU version GPU version Ionization/recombination (if on) ioniz_recomb_wrapper ioniz_recomb_cpu OpenADAS::ioniz_recomb_gpu Collisions (if on) collision_wrapper collision_cpu Collisions::collision_gpu Boris push boris_wrapper Boris::update_velocity_cpu Boris::update_velocity_gpu Step step_wrapper step_cpu step_gpu Bounds check check_bounds_wrapper Boundary::check_bounds_cpu Boundary::check_bounds_gpu Fill slots fill_slots_wrapper Slots::fill_slots_cpu Slots::fill_slots_gpu Find cell find_containing_cell_wrapper find_containing_cell_cpu find_containing_cell_gpu Record statistics record_stats_wrapper Impurity::record_stats_cpu ImpurityStats::record_stats_gpu

The loop ends once every slot is dead and no particles are left to launch. The physics of each step is described in Impurity Transport, Collisions and Ionization/Recombination.

docs.title: Particle slots
docs.text:
The particles being followed are held in a fixed number of slots (Slots::Slots, src/slots.cpp). There are min(slot_cap, imp_num) of them. When a particle dies (it's absorbed at a boundary, or exceeds imp_max_time), its slot is refilled with a new particle in the fill slots step, until all of this rank's particles have been launched. The slots are stored as a structure of arrays: one array per quantity (t, x, vX, q, state, ...), indexed by slot. This is what lets each GPU thread work on one slot with fast, contiguous memory access.

The particles are split as evenly as possible between the MPI ranks (the last rank gets the remainder), and then between the GPUs on a rank (GPU 0 gets the remainder).

docs.title: CPU and GPU code
docs.text:
Every main loop step has a CPU version and a GPU version, and a wrapper that picks between them based on the use_gpu option. The wrappers are in src/impurity_transport.cpp, and they all look like this:

void step_wrapper(...)
{
#ifdef USE_CUDA
    if (opts.use_gpu_int() > 0)
    {
        // Defined in impurity_transport.cu
        step_gpu(slots_d, opts.imp_time_step(), opts_d, warnings_d.max_time);
        return;
    }
#endif

    // Defined above
    step_cpu(slots, bkg, opts, opts.imp_time_step(), max_time_ctr);
}

The physics is the same either way. The two versions are kept as close to each other as possible, so a change to one usually needs the same change in the other.

docs.title: CPU (OpenMP)
docs.text: The CPU versions loop over the slots with #pragma omp parallel for. Each OpenMP thread has its own random number generator.

docs.title: GPU (CUDA)
docs.text:
The GPU versions are split into a kernel (e.g., step_kernel) that runs one thread per slot, and a host function (e.g., step_gpu) that launches it in blocks of 256 threads. Launches are asynchronous, except in DEBUG builds, where each one waits for the kernel to finish and checks for errors. Each slot has its own random number generator (init_rngs.cu).

Kernels can't use the host-side classes, so the data they need is copied to the GPU into plain structs of device pointers:

Host side Device side Copied with Background::Background Background::BackgroundDevice Background::to_device Slots::Slots Slots::SlotsDevice Slots::to_device Impurity::Statistics ImpurityStats::StatisticsDevice Statistics::to_device OpenADAS::OpenADAS OpenADAS::OpenADASDevice OpenADAS::to_device Options::Options Options::OptionsDevice* (only the options kernels use) Options::to_device

Each has a matching free_* function. The background's times, cell centers, cell edges and bounds are small and read by nearly every kernel, so they go in GPU constant memory instead (src/cuda/device_constants.cu). Constant memory is shared by everything on a GPU, so only one background can be on each GPU.

With several GPUs, follow_impurities copies everything to each GPU and runs main_loop on each in its own std::thread (gpu_worker). Counters that the GPUs add to, like the ionization/recombination and imp_max_time warnings, are kept on each GPU and summed on the host after the threads finish.

docs.title: Fields at a particle
docs.text: Interpolating the background at a particle's position and time is the most common operation in the main loop. On the GPU it's done by building a stencil once per particle (Interpolate::build_stencil_4d, in include/cuda/interpolate.cuh) and reusing it for every field. The fields are interpolated trilinearly in space and linearly in time.

docs.title: Data layout
docs.text: The background and statistics arrays are Vectors::Vector4Ds with dimensions (t, x, y, z), and the geometry arrays are Vectors::Vector3Ds with dimensions (x, y, z). Both store the data as one flattened vector in row-major order, so the last index varies fastest. The same layout is used on the GPU (Utilities::calc_4d_index_cuda) and in the netCDF output, so the data is copied as is between them.

docs.title: Namespaces
docs.text: Namespace Contents Options The Options class holding every input option, and loading them from the input file. Background The Background class holding the plasma and geometry, and read_bkg. Gkyl Reading a Gkeyll background. Test The built-in test backgrounds. Slots The particle slots, and creating new particles. ImpurityTransport follow_impurities, the main loop and the CPU/GPU wrappers. Boris The Boris push. Collisions The Nanbu collision model. OpenADAS Reading the OpenADAS rate coefficients, and ionization/recombination. Boundary The boundary conditions. Impurity The Statistics class holding the results, recording them on the CPU, and reduce_stats. ImpurityStats Recording the statistics on the GPU, and the device-side StatisticsDevice. SaveResults Writing the netCDF output file. Interpolate, Indices, Utilities Interpolation, cell lookup and other helpers. Vectors Vector3D and Vector4D. Errors fatal_error and check_cuda (see below). Timer, Constants, Nanbu Timing, physical constants and the tabulated Nanbu A(s).

docs.title: Errors
docs.text: An error that would give wrong results if the run carried on stops it with Errors::fatal_error(msg) (src/errors.cpp). It prints the message with the MPI rank and calls MPI_Abort, so every rank stops, not just the one that hit the error. Errors::check_cuda does the same for a failed CUDA call. Device code can't stop the run itself. A kernel that finds a problem the run can continue past counts it instead, and the host reports the count at the end.

docs.title: Building and testing
docs.text:
Flan is built with CMake. Every src/*.cpp file is compiled into the library, and src/cuda/*.cu too when CUDA is enabled (-DENABLE_CUDA=ON), which also defines USE_CUDA. CPU-only builds get placeholder versions of the GPU functions in the .cpp files, inside #ifndef USE_CUDA, that stop the run if they're ever called.

The unit tests in tests/ are built with the library. The *_cpu tests are always built, and the *_cuda tests only with CUDA. Run them with ctest from the build directory. The regression inputs in regression/ are full simulations of the test backgrounds, compiled against the library like any other input file.

docs.title: Adding an input option
docs.text:
An option has to be added in several places, which don't check each other:

  1. include/options.h and src/options.cpp: the member with its default, a getter and a setter. A string option also needs its control integer, set in the setter, and the setter called in initialize_control_ints.
  2. src/load_options.cpp: the option name in load_input, so it can be set from an input file.
  3. src/save_results.cpp: the option in save_input_options, so it's saved in the output file.
  4. If a kernel needs it: a field in OptionsDevice (include/options_device.h), set in Options::to_device (src/cuda/options.cu). A field that isn't set there is zero on the GPU.
  5. docs-site/docs/input-options.md: the option, its type, default and description.

docs.title: MPI Parallelism
docs.text: Flan runs on several MPI processes (ranks) by giving each one a share of the impurity particles to follow. The particles don't interact with each other, so the ranks work independently for almost the whole run. They only communicate twice: once at the start, to share the background plasma, and once at the end, to add up their results. Within each rank, the particles are followed in parallel with OpenMP threads on the CPU (see OpenMP Layout) or with the GPUs the rank can see.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
rank 0                         rank 1 ... rank N-1
------                         -------------------
load options                   load options
read background
broadcast background   ----->  receive background
follow imp_num/N particles     follow imp_num/N particles
reduce statistics      <-----  send statistics
calculate derived quantities
save <case_name>.nc

Every rank calls flan(), so every step below happens on every rank unless it says otherwise.

docs.title: Startup
docs.text:
Options. Each rank loads the options itself (Options::load_options). The input options are compiled into the input file, so every rank already has them and nothing needs to be sent.

Background. Only rank 0 reads the background (Background::read_bkg). Reading a Gkeyll background calls postgkyl through read_gkyl.py and writes intermediate files, which only needs to happen once. Rank 0 then sends it to the other ranks with Background::broadcast. That broadcasts the dimensions, the times, cell centers and cell edges, and every 3D and 4D array, using MPI_Bcast from rank 0 (Utilities::mpi_broadcast_vector and Vector3D/Vector4D::broadcast). Every rank ends up with a full copy of the background, so the memory used per rank doesn't shrink with more ranks.

OpenADAS. If ionization/recombination is on, every rank reads the OpenADAS rate files itself, one rank at a time, with an MPI_Barrier between them so they don't all read the same files at once.

docs.title: Following the particles
docs.text:
ImpurityTransport::main_loop divides imp_num between the ranks:

int parts_per_rank {opts.imp_num() / nprocs};

// Give last process the remainder.
if (rank == nprocs - 1) parts_per_rank += opts.imp_num() % nprocs;

With GPUs on, each rank divides its share again between the GPUs it can see, with GPU 0 getting the remainder. Each rank then runs the main loop on its particles with no communication. Ranks can finish at different times. They wait for each other at the reduction afterwards.

Each rank needs its own random numbers, or every rank would follow the same particles. The random number generator seeds include the rank:

Seed Stream CPU seed + rank OpenMP thread number GPU seed + rank * num_gpus + gpu slot index

With the default seed = -1 (any negative value), the clock is used instead of seed, with the rank still added, so every run is different.

docs.title: Combining the results
docs.text:
After the main loop, every rank has its own Impurity::Statistics: counts, weights and weighted sums on the background grid. These are summed onto rank 0 with Impurity::reduce_stats:

  1. Each rank packs its ten statistics arrays (counts, weights, charge, s and the six velocity components) into one buffer of doubles.
  2. MPI_Reduce with MPI_SUM adds the buffers onto rank 0.
  3. Rank 0 unpacks the sums into a new Statistics object. The other ranks get an empty one.

The statistics are sums over particles, so summing them across ranks gives exactly the same result as following every particle on one rank. Only rank 0 then calculates the density, average velocities, average charge and average s from them, saves the output file and prints the timing summary.

docs.title: Running with MPI
docs.text:
Launch Flan with your system's MPI launcher, e.g.:

OMP_NUM_THREADS=5 mpiexec -np 2 ./test_exb

or srun on a cluster (see Running Flan and Perlmutter). Each rank uses OMP_NUM_THREADS OpenMP threads, so the total number of cores used is the number of ranks times OMP_NUM_THREADS.

GPUs and ranks

Each rank uses every GPU it can see (cudaGetDeviceCount). With more than one rank on a node, limit each rank to its own GPUs (e.g., with CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES or your scheduler's GPU binding), or the ranks will share the same GPUs. One rank per node, using all of that node's GPUs, is the simplest setup.

docs.title: Testing
docs.text:
tests/test_mpi.cpp checks the MPI communication: broadcasting vectors, the Vector3D/Vector4D arrays and the full background (including the simulation bounds), and summing the statistics with reduce_stats. ctest runs it on 3 ranks. To run it by hand:

mpiexec -n 3 ./tests/test_mpi

Only rank 0 prints the full GoogleTest output. The other ranks print just their failures, tagged with the rank, e.g. [rank 1] ...: Failure. A change to what's broadcast or reduced should come with a check here.

docs.title: Things to know
docs.text:
• Output. Only rank 0 prints the startup banner, the progress updates and the timing summary. The progress updates only count rank 0's particles, which is a good estimate of the whole run since every rank has about the same number.
  • Warnings. The end-of-run warnings (ionization/recombination probability above 1, particles past imp_max_time) are printed by each rank for its own particles, not summed across ranks.
  • Errors. An error anywhere stops every rank. Errors::fatal_error calls MPI_Abort, so the other ranks don't hang waiting at the next broadcast or reduction.
  • MPI setup. The input file must call MPI_Init before flan() and MPI_Finalize after it.

docs.title: OpenMP Layout
docs.text: On the CPU, Flan follows the particles on each MPI rank in parallel with OpenMP threads. Each step of the main loop is a loop over the particle slots, and OpenMP splits that loop between the threads. This page describes how that's laid out, and how the few places where threads share something are handled. For running on several ranks, see MPI Parallelism. With GPUs on, the main loop runs on the GPUs instead and OpenMP only helps with setup.

docs.title: Threads per rank
docs.text:
The number of threads is set with OMP_NUM_THREADS, the same for every rank:

OMP_NUM_THREADS=8 ./my_case                # 1 rank, 8 threads
OMP_NUM_THREADS=8 mpiexec -n 4 ./my_case   # 4 ranks, 8 threads each

Flan prints the number it's using at startup (OMP Threads/Rank). On a cluster, bind the threads to cores so they don't move around, e.g., with OMP_PLACES=cores and OMP_PROC_BIND=spread (see Perlmutter).

docs.title: The main loop
docs.text:
Every CPU version of a main loop step (*_cpu, see Code Structure) has the same shape: a loop over the slots, split between the threads, that skips dead slots and updates each alive particle on its own:

#pragma omp parallel for
for (int i = 0; i < slots.N(); ++i)
{
    // Skip dead particles
    if (slots.state()[i] > 0) continue;

    // Update particle i
    ...
}

The particles don't interact with each other, so each thread only ever reads and writes its own slots, and no locking is needed. The default static schedule splits the slots into one contiguous block per thread, which keeps each thread's memory accesses together. The slots are stored as a structure of arrays (one array per quantity), so a thread walks through each array in order.

The parallel region starts and ends inside each step, so the threads wait for each other at the end of every step before the next one starts. The steps run in a fixed order and each depends on the one before (e.g., the Boris push needs the cells found in the previous step), so this is needed.

docs.title: Random numbers
docs.text:
Collisions, ionization/recombination, the core boundary condition and launching new particles all need random numbers. Each thread has its own PCG32 generator, so threads never share one:

#pragma omp parallel
{
    // Grab our RNG for this thread, each thread has its own (and they're
    // seeded uniquely).
    int tid = omp_get_thread_num();
    pcg32& rng = rngs[tid];

    #pragma omp for
    for (int i = 0; i < slots.N(); ++i)
    {
        ...
    }
}

follow_impurities creates one generator per thread before the main loop (omp_get_max_threads() of them). They all use the same seed (seed plus the MPI rank) but a different stream (the thread number), which gives every thread its own independent sequence. Using #pragma omp parallel and then #pragma omp for, instead of #pragma omp parallel for, is what lets each thread look up its generator once, before the loop starts.

docs.title: Shared results
docs.text:
A few things are added up across all the particles. These are the only places threads write to the same memory.

What Where How Statistics (counts, weights, velocities, charge, s) Impurity::record_stats_cpu #pragma omp atomic update on each add Ionization/recombination probability > 1 warnings OpenADAS::ioniz_recomb reduction(+:...) Particles past imp_max_time step_cpu #pragma omp atomic Dead slots Slots::fill_slots_cpu reduction(+:dead_count) Slots claimed for new particles Slots::fill_slots_cpu #pragma omp atomic capture Error messages (e.g., s = nan) Collisions::nanbu_coll #pragma omp critical around the printing

Statistics. Many particles can be in the same cell, so each add to the statistics arrays is atomic. Atomics are cheap when threads rarely add to the same cell at the same time, which is the usual case since there are many more cells than threads. The commented-out buffered version in impurity_stats.cpp gives each thread its own copy of the arrays and adds them up at the end instead. It was slower in testing, but could win when there are far more particles than cells.

Filling slots. fill_slots_cpu first counts the dead slots, and decides how many to revive (all of them, or the number of particles left to launch, whichever is smaller). Then each thread claims dead slots by incrementing a shared counter with atomic capture, and stops reviving once the counter reaches that number. That way exactly the right number of particles is launched, without a lock.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text: OpenMP is also used outside the main loop, mostly in reading the background: converting and checking the Gkeyll data in read_gkyl.cpp, filling the test backgrounds in read_test.cpp, and calculating the derived quantities in impurity_stats.cpp. These are simple parallel for loops over grid cells.

docs.title: Things to know
docs.text:
• No MPI inside parallel regions. Flan calls MPI_Init, not MPI_Init_thread, so MPI may only be called from outside OpenMP parallel regions. This is also why the nan checks in the collisions only print a warning instead of calling Errors::fatal_error, which calls MPI_Abort.
  • Reproducibility. With a fixed seed, a run isn't exactly repeatable with threads. Which thread (and so which random number sequence) handles which particle depends on the number of threads, which slots get new particles depends on the order threads reach the shared counter, and the atomic adds to the statistics happen in a different order each run, which changes the last few digits. The results are statistically the same. For a repeatable run, use one thread and one rank.
  • Adding a step. A new CPU step should follow the same pattern: a parallel for over the slots that skips dead ones, the thread's own generator if it needs random numbers, and an atomic, reduction or critical section for anything shared between particles.

docs.title: Linux Installation
docs.text: These are the steps for installing Flan on a Linux machine, such as a laptop or workstation. See the Installation overview for more on each step and on choosing between a CPU and GPU build.

docs.title: 1. Install the requirements
docs.text:
You need a C++23 compiler, CMake 3.26 or newer, MPI, git and conda. On Ubuntu, for example:

sudo apt install build-essential cmake git openmpi-bin libopenmpi-dev

If your distribution's CMake is older than 3.26, a newer one can be installed with pip install cmake or from cmake.org. For conda, Miniconda is enough.

For a GPU build, you also need an NVIDIA GPU with its driver, and the CUDA Toolkit. Check that both work with:

nvidia-smi
nvcc --version

docs.title: 2. Clone Flan
docs.text:
git clone https://github.com/shawnzamperini/flan.git
cd flan

docs.title: 3. Build the dependencies
docs.text:
From the top-level flan/ directory, run:

machines/mkdeps.linux.sh

This downloads and builds zlib, HDF5 and NetCDF in $HOME/flansoft, creates the flan conda environment with postgkyl, and writes the file that tells CMake where everything is. It takes a while. To put the dependencies somewhere else, change this line in machines/mkdeps.linux.sh before running it:

export FLANSOFT=$HOME/flansoft

Then activate the environment. Do this before building, and every time before running Flan:

conda activate flan

docs.title: 4. Build, install and test Flan
docs.text:
From the top-level flan/ directory, with the flan environment active:

For a CPU build:

mkdir build_cpu && cd build_cpu
cmake ..
make -j8
make install
ctest

For a GPU build:

mkdir build_gpu && cd build_gpu
cmake .. -DENABLE_CUDA=ON
make -j8
make install
ctest

make also creates flan/scripts/flan_setup.sh, and make install puts libflan.so in flan/lib/. ctest should end with 100% tests passed. If your GPU isn't an A100 or another Ampere GPU (compute capability 8.0 or 8.6), see Supported GPUs before building.

You're ready to set up a case, see Running Flan.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: See Troubleshooting for common problems. For anything else, contact Shawn Zamperini (zamperinis@fusion.gat.com).

docs.title: Perlmutter Installation
docs.text:
These are the steps for installing Flan on NERSC's Perlmutter. See the Installation overview for more on each step.

Perlmutter's GPU nodes have NVIDIA A100 GPUs, which the GPU build supports, so the GPU build is the one to use. It runs on Perlmutter's CPU nodes too, with use_gpu = "off". On Perlmutter, Flan is built with the Cray compiler wrappers (cc and CC), which come with Cray MPICH.

docs.title: 1. Clone Flan
docs.text:
git clone https://github.com/shawnzamperini/flan.git
cd flan

docs.title: 2. Build the dependencies
docs.text:
Load the conda module, then run the Perlmutter dependency script from the top-level flan/ directory:

module load conda
machines/mkdeps.perlmutter.sh

This builds zlib, HDF5 and NetCDF with the Cray wrappers in $HOME/flansoft, creates the flan conda environment with postgkyl, and writes the file that tells CMake where everything is. To put the dependencies somewhere else, change this line in machines/mkdeps.perlmutter.sh before running it:

export FLANSOFT=$HOME/flansoft

Then activate the environment. Do this before building, and every time before running Flan, including in job scripts:

module load conda
conda activate flan

docs.title: 3. Build, install and test Flan
docs.text:
From the top-level flan/ directory, with the flan environment active:

mkdir build_gpu && cd build_gpu
cmake .. -DENABLE_CUDA=ON
make -j8
make install

Check that the CMake output says NVIDIA GPU support enabled. make also creates flan/scripts/flan_setup.sh, and make install puts libflan.so in flan/lib/.

Run the tests on a GPU node, e.g., in an interactive job, since they need a GPU and run on several MPI ranks:

ctest

It should end with 100% tests passed.

For a CPU-only build, e.g., if you'll only use the CPU nodes, use mkdir build_cpu && cd build_cpu and cmake .. instead, then the same make, make install and ctest.

You're ready to set up a case, see Running Flan and Running on Perlmutter.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: See Troubleshooting for common problems. For anything else, contact Shawn Zamperini (zamperinis@fusion.gat.com).

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
Flan is a C++ library, libflan.so, built with CMake. Installing it takes three steps:

  1. Clone the repository.
  2. Build the dependencies and create the flan conda environment, with the script for your machine.
  3. Configure, build, install and test Flan with CMake.

The steps are the same everywhere, apart from the dependency script and a few machine-specific settings. The Linux and Perlmutter pages have the exact commands for each. This page explains the choices and what each step does.

docs.title: CPU or GPU build
docs.text:
Flan can be built two ways:

  • CPU build. Particles are followed in parallel with MPI and OpenMP. This works on any Linux machine.
  • GPU build. Everything in the CPU build, plus CUDA versions of the main loop that follow the particles on GPUs. This needs an NVIDIA GPU and the CUDA Toolkit, so it doesn't work with AMD or Intel GPUs.

A GPU build can still run on the CPU: whether a simulation uses the GPUs is chosen at run time with the use_gpu input option (see Input Options). So if your machine has an NVIDIA GPU, the GPU build is the one to use.

Supported GPUs

The GPU build is compiled for compute capability 8.0 and 8.6, which covers the NVIDIA A100 (Perlmutter) and other Ampere GPUs, such as the RTX 30 series and RTX A series. For a different GPU, change CMAKE_CUDA_ARCHITECTURES in the top-level CMakeLists.txt to your GPU's compute capability, e.g., 90 for an H100. You can find it with nvidia-smi --query-gpu=name,compute_cap --format=csv.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
Your machine needs to provide:

  • A C++ compiler that supports C++23 (GCC 11.4 has been tested)
  • CMake 3.26 or newer
  • MPI (e.g., OpenMPI, MPICH or Cray MPICH)
  • OpenMP (included with GCC)
  • git
  • conda (e.g., Miniconda) or mamba
  • An internet connection when building, to download the dependencies and GoogleTest
  • GPU build only: an NVIDIA GPU and the CUDA Toolkit (CUDA 12.8 has been tested)

zlib, HDF5 and NetCDF (C and C++) are downloaded and built by the dependency script, along with postgkyl, which Flan uses to read Gkeyll data.

docs.title: Clone the repository
docs.text:
git clone https://github.com/shawnzamperini/flan.git
cd flan

docs.title: Build the dependencies
docs.text:
Run the dependency script for your machine from the top-level flan/ directory, e.g., for a general Linux machine:

machines/mkdeps.linux.sh

This builds zlib, HDF5 and NetCDF in $HOME/flansoft (change FLANSOFT in the script to put them elsewhere). It also creates the flan conda environment, which has postgkyl and the Python packages Flan needs, and sets the environment variables Flan uses to find its Python scripts. Finally, it writes install-deps/build-opts.cmake, which tells CMake where the dependencies are. CMake won't configure without it, so the dependencies always come first.

Activate the environment before building and before running Flan:

conda activate flan

Build and run in the same environment

The flan environment includes its own MPI. Activate it before running CMake, so Flan is built with the same MPI it'll run with. Building with one MPI and running with another usually crashes at the first MPI call.

docs.title: Build Flan
docs.text:
The CPU and GPU builds each go in their own build directory, so you can have both. From the top-level flan/ directory:

1. Make a build directory and configure. CMake checks the compilers and dependencies and writes the Makefiles:

For a CPU build:

mkdir build_cpu && cd build_cpu
cmake ..

For a GPU build:

mkdir build_gpu && cd build_gpu
cmake .. -DENABLE_CUDA=ON

The output should end with -- Build files have been written to: .... For a GPU build, check that it says NVIDIA GPU support enabled.

2. Build. This compiles the library and the tests, and creates flan/scripts/flan_setup.sh, which sets up new cases (see Running Flan). -j8 builds with 8 processes. Use however many cores you have.

make -j8

3. Install.

make install

This copies libflan.so to flan/lib/, and the CMake files that cases use to find Flan to flan/lib/cmake/flan/.

One installed build at a time

Both builds install to the same flan/lib/, so the last make install is the one cases use. If you switch between a CPU and GPU build, run make install in the one you want, then rebuild your case.

4. Run the tests.

ctest

All the tests should pass:

100% tests passed, 0 tests failed out of 7

A CPU build has 7 tests. A GPU build has those plus the GPU tests, 17 in all, and they need a GPU to run on. One of the tests checks the MPI communication, so it runs Flan's test program on 3 MPI ranks. If a test fails, ctest --output-on-failure shows what went wrong.

docs.title: Build options
docs.text:
These are set with -D when configuring, e.g., cmake .. -DENABLE_CUDA=ON.

Option Default Description ENABLE_CUDA OFF Build the GPU version. Needs the CUDA Toolkit. CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE Release Release for normal use. Debug turns off optimization and turns on extra checks, e.g., the GPU waits after every kernel and prints any error. RelWithDebInfo is optimized but keeps debugging information.

docs.title: Rebuilding
docs.text:
After pulling new changes, rebuild and reinstall from the build directory:

make -j8 && make install

If files were added to or removed from Flan, run cmake .. first so CMake picks them up.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
Every machine is a little different, so problems can come up that these instructions don't cover. A few common ones:

  • CMake can't find build-opts.cmake: the dependency script hasn't been run yet, or it failed partway. Run it again and check its output.
  • CMake can't find the CUDA compiler: the CUDA Toolkit isn't installed or nvcc isn't on your PATH.
  • A crash right at the start of a run, mentioning MPI: Flan was probably built and run with different MPIs. See the note on building and running in the same environment above.

For anything else, contact Shawn Zamperini (zamperinis@fusion.gat.com), so the instructions can be updated too.

docs.title: Machine instructions
docs.text:
• Linux: any Linux machine, such as a laptop or workstation.
  • Perlmutter: NERSC's Perlmutter.

docs.title: Collisions
docs.text: Impurity ions in Flan undergo Coulomb collisions with the background ions and electrons through the Nanbu collision model. Collisions are turned on with imp_collisions = "nanbu", and are applied once per time step, just before the Boris push (see Impurity Transport).

docs.title: The Nanbu model
docs.text:
The Nanbu model was introduced in:

K. Nanbu, "Theory of cumulative small-angle collisions in plasmas," Phys. Rev. E 55, 4642–4652 (1997). doi:10.1103/PhysRevE.55.4642

A charged particle moving through a plasma undergoes a huge number of small-angle Coulomb collisions. Following each one is out of the question, and Nanbu's insight was that their cumulative effect over a time step \(\Delta t\) can be replaced by a single deflection of the relative velocity by an angle \(\chi\). The distribution of \(\chi\) depends only on one dimensionless parameter,

\[ s = \frac{\ln\Lambda}{4\pi}\left(\frac{q_a q_b}{\varepsilon_0 \mu_{ab}}\right)^2 \frac{n_b}{g^3}\,\Delta t, \]

where \(q_a\) and \(q_b\) are the charges of the impurity and the background species, \(\mu_{ab}\) is their reduced mass, \(n_b\) is the background density, \(g\) is the magnitude of their relative velocity and \(\ln\Lambda\) is the Coulomb logarithm. \(s\) is roughly the number of collision times that fit in \(\Delta t\), so it measures how collisional the step is:

  • \(s \ll 1\): the step is weakly collisional, and \(\chi\) is small.
  • \(s \gg 1\): the particle has "forgotten" its initial direction, and \(\chi\) is isotropic.

The model covers the whole range of \(s\) in one distribution, which is its main strength. A Monte Carlo collision step built on it goes smoothly from weak, small-angle scattering to full isotropization without changing algorithms.

docs.title: Implementation
docs.text: The model lives in the Collisions namespace (src/collisions.cpp, and src/cuda/collisions.cu for the GPU). Every alive, charged particle collides first with the background ions and then with the background electrons (the friction_force test case skips electron collisions). For each species, the steps are as follows.

docs.title: 1. Sample a background particle
docs.text:
The local \(n_e\), \(T_e\), \(T_i\) and flow velocity \(\mathbf{u}\) are interpolated to the particle's position and time. Each Cartesian component of a background particle's velocity is then sampled from a drifting Maxwellian:

\[ v_{b,j} \sim \mathcal{N}\!\left(u_j,\ \sqrt{T_b/m_b}\right), \]

and the relative velocity is \(\mathbf{g} = \mathbf{v}_a - \mathbf{v}_b\). The same flow velocity, from the Gkeyll ion moments, is used for both ions and electrons. The background masses come from gkyl_ion_mass_amu and gkyl_elec_mass_amu.

docs.title: 2. Calculate s
docs.text:
\(s\) is calculated with the formula above, with an impurity of charge state \(Z\) (\(q_a = Ze\)) and a singly charged background (\(q_b = e\), \(n_b = n_e\)). The instantaneous \(g\) of the sampled pair is used in \(g^3\).

The Coulomb logarithm is \(\ln\Lambda = \ln(\lambda_D / b_0)\). \(\lambda_D\) is the electron Debye length, and \(b_0\) is the impact parameter for 90° scattering evaluated at the expected value of the relative velocity, \(\langle g^2\rangle = 3T_b/\mu_{ab}\):

\[ b_0 = \frac{q_a q_b}{2\pi\varepsilon_0\,\mu_{ab}\,\langle g^2 \rangle}. \]

docs.title: 3. Calculate A
docs.text:
The shape of the \(\chi\) distribution is set by \(A(s)\), the solution of

\[ \coth A - \frac{1}{A} = e^{-s}. \]

There is no closed form for \(A\), so it is linearly interpolated from a table (include/nanbu_s_a.h, generated by python/calc_nanbu_A.py) for \(0.01 \le s \le 5\). Outside this range, the asymptotic limits are used: \(A = 1/s\) for \(s < 0.01\) and \(A = 3e^{-s}\) for \(s > 5\).

docs.title: 4. Sample the deflection angle
docs.text:
With a uniform random number \(U \in (0, 1]\), the deflection angle is sampled by inverting the cumulative distribution:

\[ \cos\chi = \frac{1}{A}\ln\!\left(e^{-A} + 2U\sinh A\right). \]

For \(s < 0.02\), the small-\(s\) limit \(\cos\chi = 1 + s\ln U\) is used, and for \(s > 6\) the deflection is isotropic, \(\cos\chi = 2U - 1\).

docs.title: 5. Update the velocity
docs.text:
\(\mathbf{g}\) is rotated by \(\chi\) about a random azimuthal angle \(\varepsilon \in [0, 2\pi)\), and the impurity velocity becomes

\[ \mathbf{v}_a' = \mathbf{v}_a - \frac{m_b}{m_a + m_b} \left[\mathbf{g}\,(1 - \cos\chi) + \mathbf{h}\sin\chi\right], \]

where \(\mathbf{h}\) is perpendicular to \(\mathbf{g}\), has the same magnitude, and points in the direction set by \(\varepsilon\). Only the impurity is updated. The background is fixed, so this is a test-particle model.

docs.title: Neutrals
docs.text: Neutrals (\(Z = 0\)) are skipped, since they don't undergo Coulomb collisions. Neutral–plasma interactions such as charge exchange or elastic scattering off background neutrals are not included in Flan.

docs.title: Safeguards
docs.text:
A few limits keep the calculation well behaved in extreme corners of the background:

Quantity Limit \(n_e\), \(T_e\), \(T_i\) At least min_ne, min_te and min_ti \(\ln\Lambda\) At least 1 \(g\) At least \(10^{-3}\) m/s, to avoid dividing by zero in \(s\) \(\cos\chi\) Clamped to \([-1, 1]\), to guard against rounding errors

docs.title: When the model is valid
docs.text:
The Nanbu model rests on a few assumptions. Each one is satisfied in typical edge and scrape-off layer plasmas, but each can break down.

Valid when:

  • The plasma is weakly coupled, \(\ln\Lambda \gg 1\). The model assumes that the deflection is dominated by many distant, small-angle collisions, the same assumption behind the Landau/Fokker–Planck collision operator. Typical edge plasmas have \(\ln\Lambda \approx 10\)–\(15\), which is well within this regime.
  • The impurities are trace. The background is treated as a fixed Maxwellian that the impurities don't modify, so momentum and energy given to the background are not fed back into it. This is fine as long as the impurity density is small compared to the plasma density.
  • The background is close to a Maxwellian. Background velocities are sampled from a drifting, isotropic Maxwellian with a single temperature, so temperature anisotropy and non-Maxwellian tails are not captured.
  • The background changes little over one time step. The plasma parameters are evaluated once at the start of the step and held fixed for the collision.

One thing the model does not require is a time step much smaller than the collision time. The \(\chi\) distribution is valid for any \(s\), which is the point of the model. In practice, Flan's time step is set by resolving the gyromotion in the Boris push, which usually makes \(s\) small anyway.

Invalid or questionable when:

  • \(\ln\Lambda\) approaches a few or less. This happens in very cold, dense plasmas, e.g., deeply detached divertor conditions. Large-angle collisions become important, and the small-angle picture is no longer accurate. If \(\ln\Lambda\) falls below 1 it's clamped to 1, so results in these regions should be treated with caution.
  • The impurity concentration is high. The impurities would noticeably change the background (and \(n_i \ne n_e\)), which the test-particle approach can't capture.
  • The background has more than one ion species, or the main ions aren't singly charged. \(q_b = e\) and \(n_b = n_e\) are assumed for the ion collisions, so collisions with other ion species, e.g., impurity–impurity collisions, are not included.
  • Neutral collisions matter. As noted above, only Coulomb collisions with charged background species are modeled.

docs.title: Impurity Transport
docs.text: Flan follows impurity ions through a background plasma (usually from Gkeyll) by integrating each particle's full orbit, including its gyromotion. No guiding-center approximation is made. Each particle is pushed through the background electric and magnetic fields with the Boris algorithm, and its charge state and velocity are updated between pushes by ionization/recombination and Coulomb collisions.

docs.title: The main loop
docs.text:
Particles are held in a fixed number of slots. Each pass through the main loop (ImpurityTransport namespace, impurity_transport.cpp) advances every alive particle in the slots by one time step, imp_time_step:

  1. Ionization/recombination (if imp_iz_recomb = "on"): the charge state may change based on OpenADAS rate coefficients. See Ionization/Recombination.
  2. Collisions (if imp_collisions = "nanbu"): the velocity is scattered by the background ions and electrons with the Nanbu model. See Collisions.
  3. Boris push: the velocity is updated from the Lorentz force (described below).
  4. Step: the position is moved forward by \(\mathbf{v}\,\Delta t\), and the particle's time is advanced.
  5. Bounds check: particles that leave the domain are absorbed, wrapped (periodic boundaries) or otherwise handled by the boundary conditions.
  6. Fill slots: the slots of dead particles are filled with newly launched particles until none are left to follow.
  7. Find cell: the grid cell and background time frame that contain each particle are found.
  8. Record statistics: each particle's contribution to the impurity density and other outputs is added to the cell it's in.

The loop runs until every slot is dead and there are no particles left to launch. A particle is also killed once it has been followed for longer than imp_max_time.

Each step has a CPU (OpenMP) and GPU (CUDA) implementation. A wrapper function picks between them based on use_gpu, so the physics is the same either way.

docs.title: Coordinates
docs.text:
The background is defined on a computational grid \((x, y, z)\) that is generally curvilinear, e.g., field-aligned coordinates. The Lorentz force is much simpler to evaluate in Cartesian space, though, so each particle carries two velocities:

  • \((v_X, v_Y, v_Z)\): the Cartesian velocity. This is what the Boris algorithm updates.
  • \((v_x, v_y, v_z)\): the velocity in computational coordinates. This is what moves the particle on the grid.

After the Cartesian velocity has been updated, the computational velocity is found with the reciprocal (contravariant) basis vectors \( abla x\), \( abla y\), \( abla z\):

\[ v_x = rac{\partial x}{\partial X} v_X + rac{\partial x}{\partial Y} v_Y + rac{\partial x}{\partial Z} v_Z \]

and similarly for \(v_y\) and \(v_z\). The basis vectors are stored at the cell centers, and are trilinearly interpolated to the particle's position.

docs.title: The Boris algorithm
docs.text: The Boris algorithm is the standard method for pushing charged particles through electric and magnetic fields. It is second-order accurate and time-reversible. A pure magnetic field does no work, and the algorithm conserves energy exactly in that case, so the gyro-orbit doesn't drift over the many gyro-periods a particle is followed for.

docs.title: Leapfrog staggering
docs.text:
Positions and velocities are staggered by half a time step (leapfrog):

\[ \mathbf{x}_n = \mathbf{x}(t_n), \qquad \mathbf{v}_n = \mathbf{v}(t_n - \Delta t/2) \]

Particles are launched with the position and velocity at the same time, so the velocity is pushed backwards by half a time step (\(-\Delta t/2\)) before the main loop starts. This sets up the staggering.

docs.title: Field interpolation
docs.text:
Before the push, \(\mathbf{E}\) and \(\mathbf{B}\) are found at the particle's position and time:

  1. Each Cartesian component, and the magnitude, is trilinearly interpolated in space between the centers of the cell containing the particle and its neighbors on the particle's side. This is done for the particle's nearest background time frame and the neighboring frame on the particle's side in time, so the particle's time is always between the two frames.
  2. The two values are linearly interpolated in time to the particle's time.
  3. The interpolated vector is rescaled to the interpolated magnitude.

Interpolation keeps the fields continuous as a particle crosses cell boundaries and background time frames. With piecewise-constant fields, particles get unphysical "kicks" at every boundary and drift off the field line (numerical diffusion). Interpolating in time also matters for time-dependent drifts like the polarization drift.

The rescaling in step 3 is a deliberate trade-off. An interpolated vector is almost always shorter than the true field, which would make the gyroradius wrong. Rescaling to the interpolated magnitude gets the gyro-orbit right, at the cost of a small discontinuity at cell boundaries. A particle spends far more time inside a cell than crossing a boundary, so getting the orbit right matters more.

docs.title: The push
docs.text:
With the charge-to-mass ratio \(q/m\) (where \(q = Z e\) for charge state \(Z\)), the velocity is advanced from \(\mathbf{v}_n\) to \(\mathbf{v}_{n+1}\):

  1. Half electric kick:

    \[ \mathbf{v}^- = \mathbf{v}_n + \frac{q}{m}\mathbf{E}\,\frac{\Delta t}{2} \]

  2. Magnetic rotation. With

    \[ \mathbf{t} = \frac{q}{m}\mathbf{B}\,\frac{\Delta t}{2}, \qquad \mathbf{s} = \frac{2\mathbf{t}}{1 + |\mathbf{t}|^2} \]

    the velocity is rotated about \(\mathbf{B}\) in two steps:

    \[ \mathbf{v}' = \mathbf{v}^- + \mathbf{v}^- \times \mathbf{t}, \qquad \mathbf{v}^+ = \mathbf{v}^- + \mathbf{v}' \times \mathbf{s} \]

  3. Second half electric kick:

    \[ \mathbf{v}_{n+1} = \mathbf{v}^+ + \frac{q}{m}\mathbf{E}\,\frac{\Delta t}{2} \]

The rotation leaves \(|\mathbf{v}^+| = |\mathbf{v}^-|\), so all energy change comes from the electric field. Finally, \((v_x, v_y, v_z)\) are calculated from the new Cartesian velocity (see Coordinates), and the step moves the particle:

\[ \mathbf{x}_{n+1} = \mathbf{x}_n + \mathbf{v}_{n+1}\,\Delta t \]

docs.title: Implementation
docs.text:
The CPU version is Boris::update_velocity_cpu in src/boris.cpp, parallelized over particles with OpenMP. The GPU version is update_velocity_kernel in src/cuda/boris.cu, with one thread per particle. The two use the same push. The GPU version builds the interpolation stencils with the helpers in include/cuda/interpolate.cuh. The core of the push is:

// Charge state times the (positive) elementary charge, divided by mass
double q_m {slots.q()[i] * -Constants::charge_e / slots.mass()};

// t vector
for (int j {}; j < 3; ++j) t[j] = q_m * B_local[j] * 0.5 * dt;
double tmag2 {t[0]*t[0] + t[1]*t[1] + t[2]*t[2]};

// s vector
for (int j {}; j < 3; ++j) s[j] = 2 * t[j] / (1.0 + tmag2);

// Half electric kick
for (int j {}; j < 3; ++j) vminus[j] = v[j] + q_m * E_local[j] * 0.5 * dt;

// Magnetic rotation
vminus_cross_t = Utilities::cross_product(vminus, t);
for (int j {}; j < 3; ++j) vprime[j] = vminus[j] + vminus_cross_t[j];
vprime_cross_s = Utilities::cross_product(vprime, s);
for (int j {}; j < 3; ++j) vplus[j] = vminus[j] + vprime_cross_s[j];

// Second half electric kick
slots.set_vX(i, vplus[0] + q_m * E_local[0] * 0.5 * dt);
slots.set_vY(i, vplus[1] + q_m * E_local[1] * 0.5 * dt);
slots.set_vZ(i, vplus[2] + q_m * E_local[2] * 0.5 * dt);

Constants::charge_e is the electron charge (\(-1.602\times10^{-19}\) C), so q * -charge_e is the positive ion charge \(Ze\).

docs.title: Neutrals
docs.text:
Neutrals are handled correctly

Particles in charge state \(Z = 0\) are followed in the same loop as the ions and need no special treatment in the Boris push. With \(q = 0\):

  • \(q/m = 0\), so both electric kicks vanish,
  • \(\mathbf{t} = \mathbf{s} = 0\), so there is no magnetic rotation,

and \(\mathbf{v}_{n+1} = \mathbf{v}_n\). A neutral moves in a straight line at constant velocity, as it should, and it isn't affected by the fields.

The other steps also treat neutrals correctly:

  • Collisions: neutrals are skipped, since they don't undergo Coulomb collisions.
  • Ionization/recombination: a neutral can ionize to \(Z = 1\) but can't recombine, so its recombination probability is zero. Once it's ionized, the next Boris push uses the new charge, and the particle starts to gyrate.

A neutral's velocity can only change when it ionizes. Until then, it just streams through the plasma.

docs.title: Ionization and Recombination
docs.text: As an impurity moves through the plasma, its charge state changes through electron-impact ionization and recombination. Flan models both as random events whose probabilities come from OpenADAS rate coefficients. They are turned on with imp_iz_recomb = "on", and are applied once per time step, at the start of each pass through the main loop (see Impurity Transport).

docs.title: Rate coefficients
docs.text:
The rate coefficients come from the OpenADAS database (open.adas.ac.uk), in ADF11 format:

  • SCD files: effective ionization rate coefficients, \(S_Z(n_e, T_e)\), for \(Z \to Z+1\).
  • ACD files: effective recombination rate coefficients, \(\alpha_{Z}(n_e, T_e)\), for \(Z \to Z-1\).

These are effective (collisional-radiative) coefficients. They depend on both \(n_e\) and \(T_e\), and they include the effect of the excited-state populations. Recombination includes radiative, dielectronic and three-body recombination.

Each file is read from

[openadas_root]/scd[openadas_year]/scd[openadas_year]_[element].dat
[openadas_root]/acd[openadas_year]/acd[openadas_year]_[element].dat

where openadas_root and openadas_year are input options (openadas_year defaults to 50) and the element is chosen with imp_atom_num. For example, tungsten with the default year reads scd50/scd50_w.dat and acd50/acd50_w.dat. The supported elements are H through Ne, Al, Si, Cl, Ar, Fe, Kr, Mo, Xe and W.

The files store \(\log_{10}\) of the densities (cm\(^{-3}\)), temperatures (eV) and rate coefficients (cm\(^3\)/s). These are converted to m\(^{-3}\), eV and m\(^3\)/s when they are read in (OpenADAS::read_rate_coefficients in src/openadas.cpp).

docs.title: Interpolation
docs.text:
For each particle, \(n_e\) and \(T_e\) are interpolated to the particle's position and time, the same way as in the Boris push. The rate coefficient for the particle's charge state is then bilinearly interpolated in \((T_e, n_e)\) from the table.

If \(n_e\) or \(T_e\) fall outside the range of the OpenADAS data, they are clamped to the nearest edge of the table. The rates are never extrapolated.

docs.title: Charge-state update
docs.text:
During one time step \(\Delta t\), a particle in charge state \(Z\) ionizes with probability

\[ P_\text{iz} = S_Z(n_e, T_e)\, n_e\, \Delta t \]

and recombines with probability

\[ P_\text{rec} = \alpha_Z(n_e, T_e)\, n_e\, \Delta t. \]

Two uniform random numbers \(U_1, U_2 \in [0, 1)\) are drawn, and the charge becomes

\[ Z \to Z + [U_1 < P_\text{iz}] - [U_2 < P_\text{rec}], \]

where \([\cdot]\) is 1 if the condition is true and 0 otherwise. If both events happen in the same step they cancel and the charge state is unchanged, so the charge changes by at most one per step.

A fully stripped ion (\(Z\) equal to the atomic number) can't ionize, so \(P_\text{iz} = 0\). The velocity is not changed by an ionization or recombination event. The new charge simply takes effect in the next Boris push and collision step.

The CPU version is OpenADAS::ioniz_recomb (src/openadas.cpp), and the GPU version is ioniz_recomb_kernel (src/cuda/openadas.cu).

docs.title: Neutrals
docs.text:
Neutrals are handled correctly

A neutral (\(Z = 0\)) can ionize to \(Z = 1\) using the \(Z = 0 \to 1\) SCD coefficient, but it can't recombine, so \(P_\text{rec} = 0\). Once it's ionized, it is pushed by the fields and starts to undergo collisions. See Impurity Transport and Collisions.

docs.title: Choosing the time step
docs.text:
\(P = R\, n_e\, \Delta t\) is the first-order expansion of the exact probability \(1 - e^{-R\, n_e\, \Delta t}\), and it's only accurate when \(P \ll 1\). The update also allows at most one ionization or recombination per step. Both mean the time step must be short compared to the ionization and recombination times, \(1/(S_Z n_e)\) and \(1/(\alpha_Z n_e)\).

If \(P > 1\), the event always happens and the true rate is underestimated. Flan counts how often this happens, and prints a warning at the end of the run:

Warning: Ionization probability was > 1.0 for N particles. Consider using a smaller time step.

(and similarly for recombination). The counter is incremented each time step that the probability is above 1, so \(N\) counts particle-steps rather than unique particles. If these warnings show up for more than a handful of particle-steps, reduce imp_time_step. This is most likely for low charge states in hot, dense plasma, where ionization is fastest.

docs.title: When the model is valid
docs.text:
Valid when:

  • The time step resolves the atomic time scales, i.e., \(P \ll 1\) (see above).
  • The plasma is within the range of the OpenADAS tables. Outside the table, the edge values are used, which can be a poor approximation, e.g., at temperatures far below the lowest tabulated \(T_e\).
  • The electrons are close to Maxwellian. The ADAS coefficients are averaged over a Maxwellian electron distribution at \(T_e\).
  • The excited states are in quasi-steady state. The effective coefficients assume that excited-state populations relax much faster than the plasma conditions change along the impurity's path. This usually holds, though long-lived metastable states can violate it.

Not included:

  • Charge-exchange recombination with background neutrals, e.g., \(W^{Z+} + D^0 \to W^{(Z-1)+} + D^+\), which can be important in regions with a high neutral density.
  • Ionization by ions or photons. Only electron-impact ionization is included.
  • More than one charge change per step. See Choosing the time step.

docs.title: Running Flan
docs.text:
A Flan simulation is a case: a directory with an input file, which is a small C++ program that sets the options and calls Flan. Running one takes four steps:

  1. Set up a case directory with flan_setup.sh.
  2. Set the options in the input file.
  3. Compile it with make.
  4. Run it, from the command line or with a job script.

This page assumes Flan is installed (see Installation). Activate the flan conda environment before any of these steps:

conda activate flan

The environment has the paths Flan needs to read Gkeyll data. A Gkeyll run without it stops with an error saying READ_GKYL_PY is not set.

docs.title: Set up a case
docs.text:
Create a case directory with the setup script, which is made when Flan is built:

/path/to/flan/scripts/flan_setup.sh my_case
cd my_case

This creates my_case/ with:

  • my_case.cpp: the input file, a copy of regression/blank_input_file.cpp to start from.
  • CMakeLists.txt and the Makefile made from it, which compile the input file against the installed Flan library.

The executable is named after the case, and it's built from the .cpp file with the same name, so keep the two names the same.

docs.title: The input file
docs.text:
The input file sets the options in create_inputs and passes them to Flan:

#include "flan.h"
#include "mpi.h"

Inputs create_inputs()
{
    Inputs inpts;

    inpts["case_name"] = "my_case";
    inpts["imp_num"] = 100000;
    inpts["imp_time_step"] = 1e-8;
    inpts["imp_atom_num"] = 74;
    inpts["imp_mass_amu"] = 183.84;
    // ... any other options

    return inpts;
}

int main(int argc, char* argv[])
{
    MPI_Init(&argc, &argv);
    Inputs inpts {create_inputs()};
    flan(inpts);
    MPI_Finalize();
}

Every option is listed on the Input Options page, and any option you don't set uses its default. The value has to have the option's type: inpts["imp_num"] = 1e5 is a double, so it stops the run for an int option, while inpts["imp_num"] = 100000 works. An option name that isn't recognized, e.g., from a typo, also stops the run, before the simulation starts.

The blank input file turns on ionization/recombination, which needs the OpenADAS rate coefficient files. These aren't installed with Flan. Download them from open.adas.ac.uk and set openadas_root to the directory they're in (see Ionization/Recombination for the layout Flan expects).

docs.title: Compile
docs.text:
make

This builds the executable my_case. Run make again after every change to the input file, and after reinstalling Flan.

docs.title: Run from the command line
docs.text:
./my_case

This runs on one MPI rank, using as many OpenMP threads as OpenMP chooses, usually one per core. To set the number of threads, e.g., to 8:

OMP_NUM_THREADS=8 ./my_case

To run on several MPI ranks, e.g., 2, with 8 threads each:

OMP_NUM_THREADS=8 mpiexec -n 2 ./my_case

Your system may use mpirun or srun instead of mpiexec. On a laptop or workstation, one rank with all the cores as threads is usually best. Several ranks are for spreading a run across the nodes of a cluster. Every rank holds its own copy of the background plasma, so more ranks on one machine use more memory, while more threads don't.

docs.title: GPUs
docs.text: With a GPU build of Flan installed, set inpts["use_gpu"] = "cuda" to follow the particles on the GPUs. Each rank uses every GPU it can see, so run one rank per node (see MPI Parallelism).

docs.title: What a run does
docs.text:
Flan prints a short banner with the version and the number of ranks and threads, then loads the options and the background. While particles are followed it prints progress updates (print_interval controls how many), and at the end, any warnings and a summary of where the time went.

The results are saved to <case_name>.nc, a netCDF file with four groups:

Group Contents input Every input option used in the run. geometry The times, the grid and the geometry of the background. background The background plasma: density, temperatures, fields and flow. output The impurity results: counts, density nz, average velocities, average charge and Nanbu s.

The 4D arrays have dimensions (time, x, y, z). The file can be read with any netCDF reader, e.g., netCDF4 in Python. The flan environment also has flan_plots, with plotting helpers for Flan output:

import flan_plots

fp = flan_plots.FlanPlots("my_case.nc")
fp.plot_frame_xy("nz", frame=0, z0=0.0)  # Impurity density at z = 0

docs.title: Gkeyll files
docs.text:
A run with a Gkeyll background reads the Gkeyll output files from gkyl_dir. Each file name starts with gkyl_casename. In the names below, <case> is gkyl_casename, <elc> and <ion> are gkyl_elec_name and gkyl_ion_name (elc and ion by default), and <n> is the frame number, for every frame from gkyl_frame_start to gkyl_frame_end.

These files are needed for every frame. Which moment files are needed depends on gkyl_moment_type:

gkyl_moment_type Files for each frame "bimaxwellian" (default) <case>-<elc>_BiMaxwellianMoments_<n>.gkyl<case>-<ion>_BiMaxwellianMoments_<n>.gkyl "maxwellian" <case>-<elc>_MaxwellianMoments_<n>.gkyl<case>-<ion>_MaxwellianMoments_<n>.gkyl "m0m1m2" <case>-<elc>_M0_<n>.gkyl<case>-<elc>_prim_moms_<n>.gkyl<case>-<ion>_prim_moms_<n>.gkyl

The potential, <case>-field_<n>.gkyl, is needed for every frame, whatever the moment type.

The geometry files are read once. They have no frame number:

File What Flan uses it for <case>-bmag.gkyl Magnetic field strength <case>-bcart.gkyl Direction of the magnetic field, in Cartesian (X, Y, Z) components <case>-b_i.gkyl Covariant components of the magnetic field direction <case>-jacobgeo.gkyl Jacobian <case>-gij.gkyl Metric coefficients, saved to the output for post-analysis <case>-dxdz.gkyl Tangent basis vectors <case>-dzdx.gkyl Reciprocal basis vectors, used to calculate the electric field and the gradient of B

For example, with gkyl_casename = "d3d" and the default species names, frame 5 needs d3d-elc_BiMaxwellianMoments_5.gkyl, d3d-ion_BiMaxwellianMoments_5.gkyl and d3d-field_5.gkyl.

From the moments, Flan reads the electron density and the electron and ion temperatures. The ion density isn't used. Only the "bimaxwellian" files have the ion parallel flow and perpendicular thermal velocity. Flan uses these to calculate the background flow, so collisions need "bimaxwellian" (see Input Options). Only Gkeyll's binary .gkyl format can be read.

Once the bkg_from_pgkyl_* files have been saved (see below), Flan doesn't read the Gkeyll files again.

docs.title: Gkeyll background files
docs.text:
The first time a case runs with a Gkeyll background, Flan reads the Gkeyll data with postgkyl and saves it as bkg_from_pgkyl_* files in the case directory. Later runs load those files directly, which is much faster.

Delete the background files after changing the background

The saved files are reused no matter what the Gkeyll options say. If you change gkyl_dir, gkyl_casename, the frames or the species, delete the bkg_from_pgkyl_* files so they're made again. Flan stops if the number of frames doesn't match, but it can't catch every change.

docs.title: Example: the ExB drift test
docs.text:
The test cases in regression/ are complete input files. To run the ExB drift test, which follows 100 particles through constant electric and magnetic fields:

/path/to/flan/scripts/flan_setup.sh test_exb
cd test_exb
cp /path/to/flan/regression/test_exb.cpp .
make
./test_exb

The copy replaces the blank input file, since it has the same name. The results are in exb.nc, named after its case_name.

docs.title: Running with a job script
docs.text:
On a cluster, compile on a login node as above, then submit the run as a job. There are example job scripts for:

  • Perlmutter
  • Omega

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: If a run stops with an Error! message, the message says what's wrong, e.g., an option name or value, a missing file or a background that doesn't match the options. For anything else, contact Shawn Zamperini (zamperinis@fusion.gat.com).

docs.title: Running on Omega
docs.text: Omega is General Atomics' cluster. Flan runs on Omega's CPU nodes, set up and compiled the same as on any Linux machine, with a few differences.

docs.title: Installing on Omega
docs.text:
Follow the Linux instructions, but build the dependencies with the Omega script:

machines/mkdeps.omega.sh

It puts the dependencies in /fusion/projects/codes/flan/$USER/flansoft instead of your home directory, and it creates the flan environment with mamba instead of conda, since Omega prefers mamba. Activate it with:

mamba activate flan

Omega has several compiler modules, and others loaded can get in the way. Load GCC 13 before building, the same as in the job script below:

module purge
module load gcc/13.x

docs.title: Job script
docs.text:
Compile the case on a login node (see Running Flan), then submit the run as a Slurm job. This script runs one MPI rank with 16 OpenMP threads:

#!/bin/bash -l
#SBATCH --job-name=my_case
#SBATCH --export=ALL
#SBATCH --nodes=1
#SBATCH --ntasks=1
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=16
#SBATCH --mem-per-cpu=15G
#SBATCH --partition=short
#SBATCH --time=00:30:00

# Other modules get in the way, purge them
module purge
module load gcc/13.x

# The flan environment is needed on the compute node too
eval "$(mamba shell hook --shell bash)"
mamba activate flan

export OMP_NUM_THREADS=$SLURM_CPUS_PER_TASK

./my_case

# Copy the results and the saved background files to the results area
export RESULTSDIR="/fusion/projects/results/flan/$USER/my_case"
mkdir -p $RESULTSDIR
cp bkg* $RESULTSDIR
cp *.nc $RESULTSDIR

Change my_case to your case name. The last few lines copy the results (<case_name>.nc) and the saved Gkeyll background files to Omega's results area, which is where results are meant to be kept.

docs.title: Submitting
docs.text:
If the script is saved as submit.sh:

sbatch submit.sh        # Submit the job
squeue -u $USER         # Check on it

Flan's output goes to slurm-<jobid>.out in the directory the job was submitted from.

See Running Flan for troubleshooting.

docs.title: Running on Perlmutter
docs.text:
On Perlmutter, compile the case on a login node (see Running Flan), then submit the run as a Slurm job. Below are example job scripts for the CPU nodes and the GPU nodes. Change --account to your NERSC project, and the executable name to your case. Copies of both are in the repository, as scripts/submit-flan-perlmutter-cpu.sbatch and scripts/submit-flan-perlmutter-gpu.sbatch.

Starting points

These scripts are a place to start, not tuned settings. The CPU script is the one Flan has been run with. The GPU script hasn't been tested yet. How many CPUs to ask for and how to bind the threads depends on the job, see NERSC's guide to process and thread affinity.

docs.title: CPU nodes
docs.text:
This script runs one MPI rank per node with 256 OpenMP threads each, on 2 nodes. --cpus-per-task counts hardware threads, and a CPU node has 128 cores with 2 hardware threads each, so 256 gives the rank the whole node:

#!/bin/bash -l
#SBATCH --job-name=my_case
#SBATCH --account=mXXXX         # Your NERSC project
#SBATCH --constraint=cpu
#SBATCH --nodes=2
#SBATCH --ntasks-per-node=1     # One MPI rank per node
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=256     # The whole node (128 cores x 2 threads)
#SBATCH --qos=regular           # debug (one node, short runs) or regular
#SBATCH --time=01:00:00

# OpenMP settings
export OMP_NUM_THREADS=$SLURM_CPUS_PER_TASK
export OMP_PLACES=cores         # Bind threads to cores
export OMP_PROC_BIND=spread     # Spread threads across cores

# Threads available to Python (postgkyl, when reading a Gkeyll background)
export NUMEXPR_MAX_THREADS=$SLURM_CPUS_PER_TASK

# The flan environment is needed on the compute node too
module load conda
conda activate flan

srun --cpu-bind=cores ./my_case

docs.title: GPU nodes
docs.text:
Each GPU node has 4 NVIDIA A100 GPUs. Flan uses every GPU a rank can see, so run one rank per node and give it all 4. Set inpts["use_gpu"] = "cuda" in the input file, and compile against a GPU build of Flan (see Perlmutter Installation).

#!/bin/bash -l
#SBATCH --job-name=my_case
#SBATCH --account=mXXXX         # Your NERSC project
#SBATCH --constraint=gpu
#SBATCH --nodes=1
#SBATCH --ntasks-per-node=1     # One MPI rank per node, using all 4 GPUs
#SBATCH --gpus-per-node=4
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=128     # The whole node (64 cores x 2 threads)
#SBATCH --qos=regular
#SBATCH --time=01:00:00

export OMP_NUM_THREADS=$SLURM_CPUS_PER_TASK
export OMP_PLACES=cores
export OMP_PROC_BIND=spread
export NUMEXPR_MAX_THREADS=$SLURM_CPUS_PER_TASK

module load conda
conda activate flan

srun --cpu-bind=cores ./my_case

A GPU node has 64 cores, so 128 hardware threads is the whole node. The OpenMP threads are still used on the GPU nodes, for reading the background and other setup.

docs.title: Submitting
docs.text:
If the script is saved as submit.sh:

sbatch submit.sh        # Submit the job
squeue -u $USER         # Check on it

Flan's output goes to slurm-<jobid>.out in the directory the job was submitted from, and the results to <case_name>.nc in the case directory. Use the debug QOS for quick tests: it's limited to short, small jobs, but usually starts much sooner.

See Running Flan for troubleshooting.

void Background::free_bkg (
