)

Frees the global memory arrays of a device-side background.

Each pointer is set to nullptr after it's freed. The constant memory variables (d_t, d_x, etc.) are not freed, since constant memory is allocated statically.

Parameters:

  • bkg_d Device-side background from Background::to_device.
  • device_id ID of the GPU the background is on.

docs.title: function read_bkg
docs.text:
Background Background::read_bkg (
    const Options::Options & opts
)

Reads in the plasma background from the source chosen by the bkg_source option.

"test" loads a hardcoded test background with Test::read_test, and "gkeyll" loads a Gkeyll simulation with Gkyl::read_gkyl. SOLEDGE3X backgrounds (control integer 2) are not implemented yet. If the source is not implemented or not recognized, the run is stopped with Errors::fatal_error. Options::set_bkg_source already rejects any other value, so this is only a safeguard.

Parameters:

  • opts Simulation options.

Returns:

Background object holding the plasma background.

docs.title: function broadcast
docs.text:
void Background::Background::broadcast (
    MPI_Comm comm
)

Broadcasts the background from rank 0 to every other MPI rank.

Every rank must call this. After it returns, every rank holds a copy of the dimensions, the simulation bounds (t, x, y and z min/max), the times and computational grid, the geometry data and the plasma and field data loaded on rank 0. Not broadcast are bR, the covariant magnetic field components (b_x, b_y, b_z) and the electric field gradient (gradeX, gradeY, gradeZ), which are only saved to the output file on rank 0.

Parameters:

  • comm MPI communicator to broadcast over.

docs.title: function check_dim
docs.text:
std::string Background::Background::check_dim (
    const int m_dim,
    const int in_dim,
    const int dim_num
)

Checks that a new dimension matches the dimension already stored.

A stored dimension of 0 means it has not been set yet, so any new dimension is accepted. Otherwise the two must be equal.

Parameters:

  • m_dim Dimension currently stored in the Background.
  • in_dim Dimension of the data being loaded.
  • dim_num Which dimension (1-4) is being checked (for the message).

Returns:

Empty if the dimensions are consistent. Otherwise a line describing the mismatch, for set_dims to put in its error message.

docs.title: function interp_4d
docs.text:
BkgFPType Background::Background::interp_4d (
    const Vectors::Vector4D < BkgFPType > & vec4d,
    const double t0,
    const double x0,
    const double y0,
    const double z0
) const

Interpolates 4D background data at a given time and position.

This is a convenience wrapper around Utilities::interp_vec4d that passes in the background times and the x, y and z cell centers, so callers only need to supply the data and the point to evaluate it at.

Parameters:

  • vec4d Data to interpolate, stored as a function of (t, x, y, z).
  • t0 Time at which to evaluate the data.
  • x0 x-coordinate at which to evaluate the data.
  • y0 y-coordinate at which to evaluate the data.
  • z0 z-coordinate at which to evaluate the data.

Returns:

Interpolated value at (t0, x0, y0, z0).

docs.title: function set_dims
docs.text:
template<typename T>
void Background::Background::set_dims (
    Vectors::Vector4D < T > & v,
    const std::string_view data
)

Checks the dimensions of a Vector4D against the stored dimensions and stores them if they are consistent.

Each of the four dimensions of v is checked with check_dim. If all four are consistent, they become the stored dimensions. If any are not, the run is stopped with Errors::fatal_error, listing every dimension that doesn't match. A mismatch means the data is not being read in correctly or is from different Gkeyll runs.

Template parameters:

  • T Data type stored in the Vector4D.

Parameters:

  • v Vector4D whose dimensions are checked.
  • data Name of the data being loaded (for the error message).

docs.title: function to_device
docs.text:
BackgroundDevice Background::Background::to_device (
    int device_id=0
)

Copies the background to a GPU.

The times, cell centers, cell edges and simulation bounds are copied to constant memory (see device_constants.cu), and the 3D and 4D arrays are allocated and copied to global memory. Constant memory is per GPU, so each GPU gets its own copy. Constant memory is shared by everything on a GPU, though, so only one background can be on each GPU at a time. Copying a second one to the same GPU overwrites the constant memory of the first.

Stops the run with Errors::fatal_error if a dimension is too big for the constant memory arrays (see MAX_1D in device_constants.cuh).

Parameters:

  • device_id ID of the GPU to copy to.

Returns:

The device-side background. Its pointers are to global memory on the GPU and must be freed with free_bkg.

docs.title: Detailed Description
docs.text:
Device-side copy of a Background, made by Background::to_device and freed with free_bkg.

The pointers are to global memory on the GPU. The 4D arrays are flattened as (t, x, y, z) and indexed with calc_4d_index_cuda, and the 3D arrays as (x, y, z) and indexed with calc_3d_index_cuda (see cuda/utilities.cuh). Vector components are in physical (Cartesian) X, Y and Z.

The times, cell centers, cell edges and simulation bounds aren't held here. They're in constant memory as the global variables d_t, d_x, d_grid_x, d_x_min, etc. (see cuda/device_constants.cuh).

Interpolates the reciprocal (contravariant) basis vectors at the particle location.

These convert a Cartesian vector into its computational components, e.g., vx = dxdX * vX + dxdY * vY + dxdZ * vZ.

Each of the nine components is trilinearly interpolated between the centers of the cell containing the particle and its neighboring cells on the side of the particle, since that is where the basis vectors are defined.

Parameters:

  • bkg Background plasma holding the basis vectors.
  • xidx x index of the grid cell containing the particle.
  • yidx y index of the grid cell containing the particle.
  • zidx z index of the grid cell containing the particle.
  • x Computational x coordinate of the particle.
  • y Computational y coordinate of the particle.
  • z Computational z coordinate of the particle.

Returns:

Interpolated components in the order dxdX, dxdY, dxdZ, dydX, dydY, dydZ, dzdX, dzdY, dzdZ.

docs.title: function update_velocity_cpu
docs.text:
void Boris::update_velocity_cpu (
    Slots::Slots & slots,
    const Background::Background & bkg,
    const Options::Options & opts,
    const double dt
)

Advances the velocity of every particle by one time step using the Boris algorithm.

The electric and magnetic fields (components and magnitudes) are trilinearly interpolated in space to the particle location, at the particle's time frame and a neighboring one, and then linearly interpolated in time. This keeps the fields continuous at cell boundaries and between time frames, which avoids numerical diffusion and unphysical kicks. Each interpolated vector is then rescaled to the interpolated magnitude so the gyro-orbit is the correct size.

The standard Boris rotation then updates the Cartesian velocity (vX, vY, vZ). Velocities are stored at the half time steps before the position, i.e., x_i = x(t_i) and v_i = v(t_i - dt/2). Finally, the velocity in computational coordinates (vx, vy, vz) is calculated with the interpolated reciprocal basis vectors from interp_recp.

Parameters:

  • slots Particle slots. The velocities are updated in place.
  • bkg Background plasma holding the fields and basis vectors.
  • opts Simulation options. Currently unused.
  • dt Time step (s).

docs.title: function update_velocity_kernel
docs.text:
void Boris::update_velocity_kernel (
    Slots::SlotsDevice slots_d,
    const Background::BackgroundDevice bkg_d,
    const double dt
)

Kernel that advances the velocity of each particle by one time step using the Boris algorithm.

One thread handles one slot, and dead particles are skipped. The electric and magnetic fields (components and magnitudes) are interpolated to the particle location, trilinear in space and linear in time, with the 4D stencil from interpolate.cuh. This keeps the fields continuous at cell boundaries and between time frames, which avoids numerical diffusion and unphysical kicks. Each interpolated vector is then rescaled to the interpolated magnitude so the gyro-orbit is the correct size. A field whose interpolated vector is zero is left as zero.

The standard Boris rotation then updates the Cartesian velocity (vX, vY, vZ). Velocities are stored at the half time steps before the position, i.e., x_i = x(t_i) and v_i = v(t_i - dt/2). Finally, the velocity in computational coordinates (vx, vy, vz) is calculated with the reciprocal basis vectors, which are interpolated in space only with the 3D stencil and are not rescaled.

Parameters:

  • slots_d Particle slots on the device. The Cartesian and computational velocities are updated in place.
  • bkg_d Background plasma on the device.
  • dt Time step (s).

docs.title: function absorbing_bc
docs.text:
int Boundary::absorbing_bc (
    double a,
    double bound,
    bool max_bound,
    double buffer
)

Checks if a value is outside an absorbing boundary.

max_bound = true means bound is a maximum and the check is a + buffer >= bound. max_bound = false means bound is a minimum and the check is a - buffer <= bound. The buffer makes the boundary trigger sooner, since the plasma can behave oddly right at the boundaries. Written without branches so it is SIMD friendly.

Parameters:

  • a Value to check (e.g., the particle's x coordinate).
  • bound Boundary value.
  • max_bound If true, bound is a maximum. Otherwise it is a minimum.
  • buffer Distance the boundary is moved inward. Defaults to 0.

Returns:

1 if the particle is outside the boundary (dead), else 0.

docs.title: function check_bounds_cpu
docs.text:
void Boundary::check_bounds_cpu (
    Slots::Slots & slots,
    const Background::Background & bkg,
    const Options::Options & opts,
    std::vector< pcg32 > & rngs
)

Checks every alive particle against the time and spatial boundaries and applies the boundary conditions (CPU implementation).

The boundaries are checked in the order t, then min/max x, y and z. Each boundary type is an integer from the *bound_type options: 0 = absorbing, 1 = periodic and 2 = core (x, y and z only). An absorbing boundary sets the slot's state and skips the remaining checks as soon as the particle is dead. For a core boundary in x, y and z are randomized, in y, z and x are randomized, and in z, x and y are randomized. The spatial buffers are the imp_*bound_buffer options, and the time boundary has no buffer. The loop over particles is parallelized with OpenMP.

Parameters:

  • slots Particle slots. The state, t and positions are updated in place.
  • bkg Background plasma, used for the simulation bounds.
  • opts Simulation options, used for the boundary types and buffers.
  • rngs Random number generators, one per OpenMP thread, used by the core boundary.

docs.title: function core_bc
docs.text:
void Boundary::core_bc (
    double & a,
    double & b,
    double & c,
    double a_min,
    double a_max,
    double a_buffer,
    double b_min,
    double b_max,
    double b_buffer,
    double c_min,
    double c_max,
    double c_buffer,
    bool max_bound,
    pcg32 & rng
)

Applies a core boundary condition.

The coordinate being checked is a, and b and c are the other two coordinates. If a is past the boundary (moved inward by a_buffer), a is put back on the buffered boundary, and b and c are moved to uniformly random values between their buffered minimums and maximums. This is like the particle entering the core and popping back out somewhere else along the core boundary. A residence time could be added if it was useful.

Parameters:

  • a Coordinate checked against the boundary.
  • b First of the other two coordinates.
  • c Second of the other two coordinates.
  • a_min Minimum of a.
  • a_max Maximum of a.
  • a_buffer Distance the a boundary is moved inward.
  • b_min Minimum of b.
  • b_max Maximum of b.
  • b_buffer Buffer on each side of the b range.
  • c_min Minimum of c.
  • c_max Maximum of c.
  • c_buffer Buffer on each side of the c range.
  • max_bound If true, check the a_max side. Otherwise check the a_min side.
  • rng Random number generator for this thread.

docs.title: function periodic_bc
docs.text:
double Boundary::periodic_bc (
    double a,
    double amin,
    double amax
)

Applies a periodic boundary condition.

A periodic boundary never kills a particle. A value above amax has the domain length (amax - amin) subtracted, and a value below amin has it added. Only a single wrap is done, so a particle is assumed to move less than one domain length per time step. Written without branches so it is SIMD friendly.

Parameters:

  • a Value to check (e.g., the particle's y coordinate).
  • amin Minimum of the domain.
  • amax Maximum of the domain.

Returns:

The wrapped value, or a unchanged if it is inside the domain.

Only a single wrap is done, so a particle is assumed to move less than one domain length per time step. Written without branches so it is SIMD friendly.

Parameters:

  • a Value to check (e.g., the particle's y coordinate).
  • amin Minimum of the domain.
  • amax Maximum of the domain.

Returns:

The wrapped value, or a unchanged if it is inside the domain.

double Collisions::nanbu_calc_A (
    const double s
)

Calculates the A term in the Nanbu collision model (Eq. 13), which sets the shape of the distribution the deflection angle is sampled from.

For s < 0.01 (weakly collisional) A = 1 / s, and for s > 5 (strongly collisional) A = 3 exp(-s). In between, A is linearly interpolated from the precomputed table in nanbu_s_a.h, which was calculated using python/calc_nanbu.py.

Parameters:

  • s The s term from nanbu_calc_s.

Returns:

The A term.

double Collisions::nanbu_calc_chi (
    const double s,
    const double A,
    pcg32 & rng
)

Samples the deflection angle chi in the Nanbu collision model (Eq. 17).

cos(chi) is found by directly inverting the cumulative distribution built from A, using a uniform random number U. For s < 0.02 the small-s limit 1 + s ln(U) is used, and for s > 6 the deflection is isotropic, 2U - 1. cos(chi) is clamped to [-1, 1] to guard against rounding errors.

Parameters:

  • s The s term from nanbu_calc_s.
  • A The A term from nanbu_calc_A.
  • rng Random number generator for this thread.

Returns:

Deflection angle chi (radians).

)

Calculates the s term in the Nanbu collision model (Eq. 19), which measures how collisional this time step is.

The relative velocity g is between the impurity and a background particle whose velocity is sampled from a drifting Maxwellian (flow plus thermal sampling) with sample_bkg_velocity. The Coulomb logarithm uses the Debye length and the expectation value of the impact parameter b0, and is clamped to be at least 1. The background species is assumed to be singly charged with ni = ne. An error is printed if the Coulomb logarithm or s is NaN.

Parameters:

  • bkg Background plasma, used to interpolate the flow velocity.
  • imp_time_step Time step (s).
  • T Temperature of the background species colliding with the impurity (eV).
  • mass_kg Mass of the background species (kg).
  • Te Electron temperature (eV), used for the Debye length.
  • ne Electron density (m^-3).
  • t Time of the particle (s).
  • x Computational x coordinate of the particle.
  • y Computational y coordinate of the particle.
  • z Computational z coordinate of the particle.
  • vX Cartesian X velocity of the impurity (m/s).
  • vY Cartesian Y velocity of the impurity (m/s).
  • vZ Cartesian Z velocity of the impurity (m/s).
  • q Charge state of the impurity. Must not be 0.
  • slots Particle slots, used for the impurity mass.
  • rng Random number generator for this thread.

Returns:

{s, gX, gY, gZ}, where gX, gY and gZ are the Cartesian components of the relative velocity (m/s).

docs.title: function nanbu_coll
docs.text:
void Collisions::nanbu_coll (
    Slots::Slots & slots,
    const Background::Background & bkg,
    const Options::Options & opts,
    bool elec,
    const double dt,
    Impurity::Statistics & imp_stats,
    std::vector< pcg32 > & rngs
)

Updates the Cartesian velocity of every particle due to Coulomb collisions with one background species using the Nanbu model.

Dead and neutral particles are skipped. For each particle, ne and Te (and Ti for ions) are interpolated at the particle location, then s, A and chi are calculated and the velocity is updated with nanbu_post_coll. Since this happens after the Boris update, the updated velocity is v at n+1/2. An error is printed if ne < 0 or chi is NaN.

For ion collisions, s * weight * dt is also added to imp_stats so the average s in each cell can be calculated later.

Parameters:

  • slots Particle slots. The velocities are updated in place.
  • bkg Background plasma.
  • opts Simulation options, used for the background masses (gkyl_elec_mass_amu, gkyl_ion_mass_amu) and min_ti.
  • elec If true, collide with electrons (Te). Otherwise collide with ions (Ti, limited to at least min_ti).
  • dt Time step (s).
  • imp_stats Impurity statistics, where the s values are summed for ion collisions.
  • rngs Random number generators, one per OpenMP thread.

void Collisions::nanbu_coll_kernel (
    Slots::SlotsDevice slots_d,
    const Background::BackgroundDevice bkg_d,
    bool elec,
    const double dt,
    ImpurityStats::StatisticsDevice stats_d,
    pcg32 * rngs_d,
    const double elec_mass_amu,
    const double ion_mass_amu,
    const Options::OptionsDevice * opts_d
)

Kernel that updates the Cartesian velocity of each particle due to Coulomb collisions with one background species using the Nanbu model.

One thread handles one slot, and dead particles are skipped. ne, Te (and Ti for ions) are interpolated at the particle location and held at or above min_ne, min_te and min_ti. Then s, A and chi are calculated and the velocity is updated with nanbu_post_coll_cuda. Since this happens after the Boris update, the updated velocity is v at n+1/2. A message is printed if chi is NaN.

Parameters:

  • slots_d Particle slots on the device. The velocities are updated in place.
  • bkg_d Background plasma on the device.
  • elec If true, collide with electrons (Te). Otherwise collide with ions (Ti).
  • dt Time step (s).
  • stats_d Impurity statistics on the device. Currently unused, since recording s is commented out.
  • rngs_d Random number generators on the device, one per slot.
  • elec_mass_amu Electron mass (amu).
  • ion_mass_amu Main ion mass (amu).
  • opts_d Simulation options on the device, used for min_ne, min_te and min_ti.

docs.title: function fatal_error
docs.text:
void Errors::fatal_error (
    const std::string & msg
)

Prints an error message and stops the whole run.

Use this for errors that would give wrong results if Flan kept going. The message is printed to stderr with the MPI rank, then MPI_Abort ends every rank. std::exit would only end this rank, and the others would hang at the next collective. If MPI isn't initialized (e.g., in the unit tests), std::exit is used instead, since MPI_Abort can't be called before MPI_Init.

Parameters:

  • msg Description of the error. "Error! " is added to the front and a newline to the end.

docs.title: function calc_bkg_flow
docs.text:
void Gkyl::calc_bkg_flow (
    grid_data_t & grid_data,
    Vectors::Vector4D < BkgFPType > & gkyl_uz,
    Vectors::Vector4D < BkgFPType > & gkyl_uX,
    Vectors::Vector4D < BkgFPType > & gkyl_uY,
    Vectors::Vector4D < BkgFPType > & gkyl_uZ,
    const Vectors::Vector4D < BkgFPType > & gkyl_bX,
    const Vectors::Vector4D < BkgFPType > & gkyl_bY,
    const Vectors::Vector4D < BkgFPType > & gkyl_bZ,
    Vectors::Vector4D < BkgFPType > & gkyl_eX,
    Vectors::Vector4D < BkgFPType > & gkyl_eY,
    Vectors::Vector4D < BkgFPType > & gkyl_eZ,
    Vectors::Vector4D < BkgFPType > & gkyl_dbdX,
    Vectors::Vector4D < BkgFPType > & gkyl_dbdY,
    Vectors::Vector4D < BkgFPType > & gkyl_dbdZ,
    Vectors::Vector4D < BkgFPType > & gkyl_viperp_sq,
    const Options::Options & opts
)

Calculates the Cartesian components of the background ion flow.

The flow is the projection of the parallel-to-z flow onto the magnetic field direction, plus the ExB drift, E x B / B^2, plus the grad-B drift, (m v_perp^2 / (2 q B^3)) B x grad(B). The ions are assumed to be singly charged.

Parameters:

  • grid_data Tuple of the time and grid vectors (see read_gkyl).
  • gkyl_uz Ion flow parallel to z (m/s).
  • gkyl_uX Array the X component of the flow (m/s) is stored in.
  • gkyl_uY Array the Y component of the flow (m/s) is stored in.
  • gkyl_uZ Array the Z component of the flow (m/s) is stored in.
  • gkyl_bX Magnetic field X component (T).
  • gkyl_bY Magnetic field Y component (T).
  • gkyl_bZ Magnetic field Z component (T).
  • gkyl_eX Electric field X component (V/m).
  • gkyl_eY Electric field Y component (V/m).
  • gkyl_eZ Electric field Z component (V/m).
  • gkyl_dbdX X component of grad(B) (T/m).
  • gkyl_dbdY Y component of grad(B) (T/m).
  • gkyl_dbdZ Z component of grad(B) (T/m).
  • gkyl_viperp_sq Ion perpendicular thermal velocity squared (m^2/s^2).
  • opts Simulation options, used for the ion mass.

docs.text:
template<typename T>
void Gkyl::calc_gradients (
    grid_data_t & grid_data,
    const Vectors::Vector4D < BkgFPType > & gkyl_vp,
    Vectors::Vector4D < BkgFPType > & gkyl_eX,
    Vectors::Vector4D < BkgFPType > & gkyl_eY,
    Vectors::Vector4D < BkgFPType > & gkyl_eZ,
    Vectors::Vector4D < BkgFPType > & gkyl_emag,
    const Vectors::Vector4D < BkgFPType > & gkyl_bmag,
    Vectors::Vector4D < BkgFPType > & gkyl_dbdX,
    Vectors::Vector4D < BkgFPType > & gkyl_dbdY,
    Vectors::Vector4D < BkgFPType > & gkyl_dbdZ,
    const Vectors::Vector4D < T > & gkyl_dxdX,
    const Vectors::Vector4D < T > & gkyl_dxdY,
    const Vectors::Vector4D < T > & gkyl_dxdZ,
    const Vectors::Vector4D < T > & gkyl_dydX,
    const Vectors::Vector4D < T > & gkyl_dydY,
    const Vectors::Vector4D < T > & gkyl_dydZ,
    const Vectors::Vector4D < T > & gkyl_dzdX,
    const Vectors::Vector4D < T > & gkyl_dzdY,
    const Vectors::Vector4D < T > & gkyl_dzdZ,
    const Options::Options & opts
)

Calculates the electric field and the magnetic field gradient in Cartesian coordinates.

The gradients of the potential and the magnetic field magnitude are first calculated in computational coordinates with central differences (forward or backward differences at the edges), assuming a uniform grid. They are then converted to Cartesian components using the reciprocal basis vectors (Eq. 2.6.35 in D'haeseleer), with E = -grad(Vp). The basis vectors are taken from the first time slice.

Template parameters:

  • T Floating-point type of the basis vectors.

Parameters:

  • grid_data Tuple of the time and grid vectors (see read_gkyl).
  • gkyl_vp Plasma potential (V).
  • gkyl_eX Array the electric field X component (V/m) is stored in.
  • gkyl_eY Array the electric field Y component (V/m) is stored in.
  • gkyl_eZ Array the electric field Z component (V/m) is stored in.
  • gkyl_emag Array the electric field magnitude (V/m) is stored in.
  • gkyl_bmag Magnetic field magnitude (T).
  • gkyl_dbdX Array the X component of grad(B) (T/m) is stored in.
  • gkyl_dbdY Array the Y component of grad(B) (T/m) is stored in.
  • gkyl_dbdZ Array the Z component of grad(B) (T/m) is stored in.
  • gkyl_dxdX Reciprocal basis vector component dx/dX.
  • gkyl_dxdY Reciprocal basis vector component dx/dY.
  • gkyl_dxdZ Reciprocal basis vector component dx/dZ.
  • gkyl_dydX Reciprocal basis vector component dy/dX.
  • gkyl_dydY Reciprocal basis vector component dy/dY.
  • gkyl_dydZ Reciprocal basis vector component dy/dZ.
  • gkyl_dzdX Reciprocal basis vector component dz/dX.
  • gkyl_dzdY Reciprocal basis vector component dz/dY.
  • gkyl_dzdZ Reciprocal basis vector component dz/dZ.
  • opts Simulation options.

docs.title: function check_tdim
docs.text:
void Gkyl::check_tdim (
    Vectors::Vector4D < BkgFPType > & gkyl_arr,
    const Options::Options & opts
)

Checks that the number of frames in the loaded background matches that requested for the simulation, stopping the run with Errors::fatal_error if not.

This only needs to be run once. It is useful if the user is reusing an already calculated background, but changed the frames in the input file. In that case the background files should be deleted so that they can be regenerated, since the default is to read any existing files. Note you can circumvent this error checking if the range of frames stays the same, but that's a fringe case and not worth the effort to protect against at the moment.

Parameters:

  • gkyl_arr Any loaded array with dimensions (t, x, y, z).
  • opts Simulation options, used for gkyl_frame_start and gkyl_frame_end.

docs.text:
void Gkyl::gradient_ybound_fix (
    grid_data_t & grid_data,
    Vectors::Vector4D < BkgFPType > & ecomp
)

Applies a fix to the y boundaries of gradient-calculated data, where the gradient generally messes up due to not as many points around.

The y boundaries are treated as periodic, and the first and last cells in y are replaced with weighted averages of the second and second to last cells. This is generally a hack, since it is not clear what to do in this situation. Ideally, the gradient calculation would handle this, but I haven't been able to figure it out. Currently unused.

Parameters:

  • grid_data Tuple of the time and grid vectors (see read_gkyl).
  • ecomp Gradient-calculated data to fix in place.

docs.title: function read_data_pgkyl
docs.text:
template<typename T>
void Gkyl::read_data_pgkyl (
    const std::string & species,
    const std::string & data_type,
    grid_data_t & grid_data,
    Vectors::Vector4D < T > & gkyl_data,
    const Options::Options & opts,
    const double species_mass_amu,
    const bool force_load
)

Reads in a Gkeyll dataset using a python interface to postgkyl, read_gkyl.py.

Species-specific data (density, temperature, par_flow and vperp_sq) is saved to bkg_from_pgkyl_[species]_[data_type].bin, and everything else to bkg_from_pgkyl_[data_type].bin. If that file already exists it is loaded directly, unless force_load is true. Otherwise read_gkyl.py is called to create it. The magnetic field and geometry files don't include the DG interpolation settings, so for those the settings saved when an earlier dataset was loaded are passed to read_gkyl.py.

Either way, the times, grid edges and cell centers in grid_data are also loaded.

Template parameters:

  • T Floating-point type of the values.

Parameters:

  • species Name of the Gkeyll species. Not used by data that isn't species-specific.
  • data_type Name of the dataset to load, e.g., density, temperature, potential or magnetic_magnitude.
  • grid_data Tuple of the time and grid vectors (see read_gkyl).
  • gkyl_data Array the values are moved into, with dimensions (t, x, y, z).
  • opts Simulation options.
  • species_mass_amu Mass of the species (amu), needed to calculate the temperature.
  • force_load If true, call read_gkyl.py even if the file already exists.

docs.title: function read_gkyl
docs.text:
Background::Background Gkyl::read_gkyl (
    const Options::Options & opts
)

Entry point for reading Gkeyll data into Flan.

Each needed dataset is loaded from the Gkeyll case, either by calling read_gkyl.py through postgkyl or, if they already exist, from the files it saved on a previous run. The electric field and magnetic field gradient are then calculated, along with the background flow if the moments are BiMaxwellian. Finally every array is moved (not copied) into a Background object.

Time-dependent data is 4D with dimensions (t, x, y, z). Time- independent data (the Jacobian, metric coefficients, basis vectors and covariant components of the magnetic field) is read in as 4D, and a single time slice is stored as 3D (x, y, z). In both cases the arrays are indexed according to the Gkeyll computational coordinate indices.

This file uses the convention that all variable names are lowercase, except x,y,z always refers to computational (Gkeyll, curvilinear) coordinates and X,Y,Z always refers to physical (Cartesian) coordinates.

Parameters:

  • opts Simulation options.

Returns:

Background object holding the Gkeyll data.

docs.text:
template<typename T>
void Gkyl::read_magnetic_field (
    grid_data_t & grid_data,
    Vectors::Vector4D < T > & gkyl_bX,
    Vectors::Vector4D < T > & gkyl_bY,
    Vectors::Vector4D < T > & gkyl_bZ,
    Vectors::Vector4D < T > & gkyl_bR,
    Vectors::Vector4D < T > & gkyl_bmag,
    const Options::Options & opts
)

Reads in the magnetic field and calculates its Cartesian components.

Gkeyll provides the Cartesian components of the magnetic field unit vector and the magnitude. The unit vector is not guaranteed to have a magnitude of 1.0 at the cell centers, so each one is renormalized to 1.0 and then multiplied by the magnitude. The number of unit vectors with a magnitude outside [0.95, 1.05] is printed. bR is the magnitude of the X-Y components.

docs.title: function record_stats_cpu
docs.text:
void Impurity::record_stats_cpu (
    Statistics & imp_stats,
    const Slots::Slots & slots,
    const Options::Options & opts,
    const double dt
)

Records the statistics of every alive particle into its cell and time frame.

For each particle, the count is incremented and weight * dt (the occupancy, in number of particles) is added to the weights. The velocities and charge are added multiplied by weight * dt, so they can later be turned into weighted averages.

Every thread writes straight into the shared arrays with atomic updates. In my basic testing this approach is much faster than the buffered approach (commented out above), though it's possible the buffered approach wins ground when there are significantly more particles than grid cells. That's because in that case particles may be fighting over accumulating stats in a cell, which can get held up in the atomics here. I am partial to the atomic approach just because it's so much cleaner.

Parameters:

  • imp_stats Statistics to record into.
  • slots Particle slots.
  • opts Simulation options. Currently unused.
  • dt Time step (s).

docs.title: function calc_density

void Impurity::Statistics::calc_density (
    const Background::Background & bkg,
    const int tot_imp_num,
    const double imp_source_scale_fact=1.0
)

Calculates the impurity density in each cell and time frame from the weights.

The weights were accumulated as weight * dt, so they are already in number of particles, and the particle weights were normalized by the number of particles when each particle was created. The density is then just the weight divided by the cell volume in physical space, J * dx * dy * dz. The density array is allocated here.

docs.title: function record_stats_kernel
docs.text:
void ImpurityStats::record_stats_kernel (
    StatisticsDevice stats_d,
    Slots::SlotsDevice slots_d,
    double dt
)

Kernel that adds each alive particle to the statistics of its cell and time frame, one thread per slot.

The count is incremented and weight * dt (the occupancy, in number of particles) is added to the weights. The Cartesian and computational velocities and the charge are added multiplied by weight * dt, so they can later be turned into weighted averages. Dead slots are skipped. The cell and time frame are the particle's tidx, xidx, yidx and zidx, so find_containing_cell_gpu must have been called first.

Parameters:

  • stats_d Impurity statistics on the device. Added to.
  • slots_d Particle slots on the device.
  • dt Time step (s).

docs.title: Detailed Description
docs.text:
Device-side copy of the impurity statistics arrays, made by Statistics::to_device and freed with free_stats.

Each array is 4D, (t, x, y, z) on the background grid, flattened the same way as the background (see calc_4d_index_cuda). Each alive particle adds to the cell and time frame it's in every time step (see record_stats_kernel). Apart from counts, every value is added multiplied by the particle's weight * dt, so dividing by weights gives the weighted average.

docs.title: function find_containing_cell_cpu
docs.text:
void ImpurityTransport::find_containing_cell_cpu (
    Slots::Slots & slots,
    const Background::Background & bkg
)

Finds the background time index and spatial cell indices for every particle in slots (CPU implementation).

Time and space are handled differently. The background times are stored at "time centers" rather than on a grid, so the time index is the index of the background time nearest to the particle's time. The spatial coordinates are defined by grid edges, so each spatial index is the index of the cell that contains the particle's x, y and z coordinates. Particles outside the grid are assigned the first or last cell in that dimension.

The indices are written back into slots with set_tidx, set_xidx, set_yidx and set_zidx. The loop over particles is parallelized with OpenMP. Every slot is updated, including slots holding dead particles.

Parameters:

  • slots Particle slots whose positions are read and whose time and cell indices are updated.
  • bkg Background plasma that provides the time array and the x, y and z grid edges.

Follows every impurity particle through the background plasma and returns the accumulated statistics.

This is the top-level driver for impurity transport. It sets up the impurity statistics arrays, loads the OpenADAS rate coefficients (one MPI rank at a time, to avoid every rank reading the same files at once) and allocates the particle slots, with min(slot_cap, imp_num) slots. All slots start dead so the first fill launches particles into them.

On GPUs, the data is copied to each GPU, a random number generator is set up for each GPU thread, and gpu_worker runs main_loop on every GPU concurrently. The statistics and timers from each GPU are then combined and the device memory is freed. On CPUs, one random number generator is created per OpenMP thread and main_loop is called directly. If GPU acceleration was requested in a build without CUDA, it is turned off.

If the seed option is negative, random number generators are seeded from the clock so each run is different. Otherwise the seed option is used. In both cases the MPI rank is added to the seed so each rank gets a different sequence.

Parameters:

  • bkg Background plasma to follow the particles through.
  • opts Simulation options. use_gpu may be turned off if Flan was built without GPU support.
  • timer Timer that accumulates the time spent in each step.

Returns:

Impurity statistics accumulated from every particle followed on this rank.

    int & max_time_ctr

Runs the main particle-following loop until every particle has been launched and followed until it dies.

The imp_num particles are split evenly between the MPI ranks, with the remainder going to the last rank. When running on GPUs, each rank's share is split again between its GPUs, with the remainder going to device 0. The slots are then filled, and the starting velocities are pushed back half a time step as the Boris algorithm requires. Each iteration of the loop then:

  • Updates charge states from ionization/recombination (if imp_iz_recomb is on).
  • Applies collisions (if imp_collisions is on).
  • Updates velocities with the Boris algorithm.
  • Advances particle positions.
  • Checks the time and spatial bounds.
  • Replaces dead particles with new ones.
  • Finds the containing cell of each particle.
  • Records statistics.

Each step is timed with a scoped timer. Progress is printed by rank 0 and GPU device 0 only.

void ImpurityTransport::step_cpu (
    Slots::Slots & slots,
    const Background::Background & bkg,
    const Options::Options & opts,
    const double dt,
    int & max_time_ctr
)

Advances every alive particle in slots by one time step (CPU implementation).

Each alive particle's time since launch (pt) and background time (t) are increased by dt, and its x, y and z positions are advanced using its current velocity. If the particle's time since launch exceeds the imp_max_time option, the particle is marked dead and max_time_ctr is incremented. The iteration counter of each stepped particle is also incremented. Dead particles are skipped. The loop over particles is parallelized with OpenMP.

Parameters:

  • slots Particle slots to advance.
  • bkg Background plasma (currently unused).
  • opts Simulation options, used for imp_max_time.
  • dt Time step (s).
  • max_time_ctr Counter of particles that exceeded the maximum allowed time. Incremented atomically.

Kernel that advances each alive particle by one time step, one thread per slot.

The time since launch pt and the background time t are increased by dt, and x, y and z are moved by the computational velocity (vx, vy, vz) times dt. If pt is then past the imp_max_time option, the particle is killed and counted in max_time_ctr_d. Dead slots are skipped. Unlike step_cpu, the iteration count isn't updated.

  • max_time_ctr_d Device counter of particles killed for exceeding imp_max_time. Incremented atomically.

docs.title: Detailed Description
docs.text:
Indices and geometry of the box of cell centers surrounding a point, used to interpolate fields at that point.

The same struct is used for 3D and 4D fields. A 3D stencil from build_stencil_3d leaves the time members (idx1, tidx_neighbor, t0 and frame_dt) unset.

The 8 corners are ordered by (x, y, z) offset as 000, 001, 010, 011, 100, 101, 110, 111, where 0 is the containing cell's index and 1 is the neighbor's index in that direction.

docs.title: function calc_ioniz_recomb_probs
docs.text:
void OpenADAS::calc_ioniz_recomb_probs (
    const OpenADASDevice & oa_ioniz_d,
    const OpenADASDevice & oa_recomb_d,
    const float ne,
    const float te,
    const float dt,
    int q,
    int Z,
    float & ioniz_prob,
    float & recomb_prob
)

Calculates the probabilities of a particle ionizing and recombining during one time step.

The rate coefficients are bilinearly interpolated in Te and ne, and the probability is rate * ne * dt. The ionization rate for charge q is at charge index q (q -> q+1), and the recombination rate is at charge index q-1 (q -> q-1). A fully stripped particle (q = Z) can't ionize and a neutral (q = 0) can't recombine, so those probabilities are zero. The probabilities are not capped at 1.

Parameters:

  • oa_ioniz_d Device-side OpenADAS struct with the ionization (SCD) rate coefficients.
  • oa_recomb_d Device-side OpenADAS struct with the recombination (ACD) rate coefficients.
  • ne Electron density at the particle location (m^-3).
  • te Electron temperature at the particle location (eV).
  • dt Time step (s).
  • q Charge state of the particle.
  • Z Atomic number of the impurity.
  • ioniz_prob Probability of ionizing this time step.
  • recomb_prob Probability of recombining this time step.

docs.title: function ioniz_recomb
docs.text:
void OpenADAS::ioniz_recomb (
    Slots::Slots & slots,
    const Background::Background & bkg,
    const OpenADAS & oa_ioniz,
    const OpenADAS & oa_recomb,
    const double dt,
    int & ioniz_warnings,
    int & recomb_warnings,
    std::vector< pcg32 > & rngs
)

Updates the charge state of every particle due to ionization and recombination.

For each particle, a random number is drawn for each process and the process occurs if it is less than its probability from calc_ioniz_recomb_probs. If both occur they cancel out and the charge is unchanged. Probabilities greater than 1 mean a smaller time step should be used if they happen often, so they are counted in ioniz_warnings and recomb_warnings.

Parameters:

  • slots Particle slots. The charges are updated in place.
  • bkg Background plasma.
  • oa_ioniz OpenADAS ionization (scd) rate coefficients.
  • oa_recomb OpenADAS recombination (acd) rate coefficients.
  • dt Time step (s).
  • ioniz_warnings Incremented by the number of particles with an ionization probability greater than 1.
  • recomb_warnings Incremented by the number of particles with a recombination probability greater than 1.
  • rngs Random number generators, one per OpenMP thread.

docs.title: function ioniz_recomb_gpu
docs.text:
void OpenADAS::ioniz_recomb_gpu (
    Slots::SlotsDevice & slots_d,
    const Background::BackgroundDevice & bkg_d,
    const OpenADASDevice & oa_ioniz_d,
    const OpenADASDevice & oa_recomb_d,
    const double dt,
    const IonizRecombWarningsDevice & warnings_d,
    pcg32 * rngs_d
)

Launches ioniz_recomb_kernel to update the charge state of every particle on the GPU due to ionization and recombination.

Uses blocks of 256 threads, one thread per slot. The warning counters are allocated once with alloc_warnings and accumulate over the whole run, so this is just a kernel launch with no allocations or copies. The launch is asynchronous, except in DEBUG builds, where it waits for the kernel to finish and prints any error. The number of particles whose ionization or recombination probability exceeded 1 is added to the counters in warnings_d.

Parameters:

  • slots_d Particle slots on the device. The charge states are updated in place.
  • bkg_d Background plasma on the device.
  • oa_ioniz_d Device-side OpenADAS struct with the ionization (SCD) rate coefficients.
  • oa_recomb_d Device-side OpenADAS struct with the recombination (ACD) rate coefficients.
  • dt Time step (s).
  • warnings_d Device-side warning counters from alloc_warnings.
  • rngs_d Random number generators on the device, one per slot.

docs.title: function ioniz_recomb_kernel
docs.text:
void OpenADAS::ioniz_recomb_kernel (
    Slots::SlotsDevice slots_d,
    const Background::BackgroundDevice bkg_d,
    OpenADASDevice oa_ioniz_d,
    OpenADASDevice oa_recomb_d,
    const float dt,
    pcg32 * rngs_d,
    int * d_ioniz_warnings,
    int * d_recomb_warnings
)

Kernel that updates the charge state of each particle due to ionization and recombination.

One thread handles one slot, and dead particles are skipped. ne and Te are interpolated at the particle location (trilinear in space between the neighboring cell centers, then linear in time), and the ionization and recombination probabilities are calculated with calc_ioniz_recomb_probs. Each is compared to its own uniform random number, so the charge changes by +1, -1 or 0 (if the particle both ionizes and recombines, the two cancel). A warning counter is incremented each time a probability exceeds 1, since that means dt is too large.

Parameters:

  • slots_d Particle slots on the device. The charge states are updated in place.
  • bkg_d Background plasma on the device.
  • oa_ioniz_d Device-side OpenADAS struct with the ionization rate coefficients.
  • oa_recomb_d Device-side OpenADAS struct with the recombination rate coefficients.
  • dt Time step (s).
  • rngs_d Random number generators on the device, one per slot.
  • d_ioniz_warnings Device counter of ionization probabilities greater than 1.
  • d_recomb_warnings Device counter of recombination probabilities greater than 1.

docs.title: function read_rate_coefficients
docs.text:
void OpenADAS::OpenADAS::read_rate_coefficients (
    std::ifstream & openadas_stream
)

Reads in the header, densities, temperatures and rate coefficients from an OpenADAS file, storing them in the class.

The densities and temperatures are stored in the file as log10(ne [cm^-3]) and log10(Te [eV]), and the rate coefficients as log10(rate [cm^3/s]). They are converted to ne (m^-3), Te (eV) and rate (m^3/s). The rates are stored with dimensions (charge, Te, ne). The run is stopped with Errors::fatal_error if the file doesn't cover every charge state (1 to Z), since the rates would be indexed incorrectly, or if there are fewer than two densities or temperatures, since the bilinear interpolation needs at least two of each.

Parameters:

  • openadas_stream Open file stream of the OpenADAS file.

docs.title: function to_device
docs.text:
OpenADASDevice OpenADAS::OpenADAS::to_device (
    int device_id
)

Copies the OpenADAS rate coefficient data to a GPU.

The scalar metadata (atomic number, table dimensions and charge range) is copied into the returned struct, and the Te grid, ne grid and flattened rate coefficient table are allocated on the device and copied over. The rates are stored by charge, then Te, then ne, so each charge state is a contiguous ntemp * ndens slice. The returned struct must be freed with free_oa. If USE_CUDA is not defined, nothing is copied and a zero-initialized struct is returned.

Parameters:

  • device_id ID of the GPU to copy the data to.

Returns:

Struct holding the metadata and device pointers to the data.

Checks that the options are compatible with each other, changing them if needed.

Currently this checks that: * Nanbu collisions are used with BiMaxwellian moments from Gkeyll. If not, collisions are turned off. * A periodic x, y or z boundary is periodic on both the minimum and maximum side. If only one side is, both are set to periodic. * GPU acceleration is off in a CPU-only build.

A warning is printed whenever an option is changed. Placeholders are left for checks of particle splitting and the variable time step.

docs.text: Default values for every option are included in the definitions of each member variable. These can then be overwritten as in load_options.cpp

docs.title: function Options
docs.text:
Options::Options::Options ()

Constructs an Options object with every option at its default value.

The defaults are set where each member variable is declared in options.h. The control integers are then set to match the default string options by calling initialize_control_ints.

docs.title: function get_control_int
docs.text:
int Options::Options::get_control_int (
    const std::string & var_name,
    const int control_int
) const

Returns a control integer after checking that it was set.

Control integers start at -1, meaning not set. If control_int is still negative, the run is stopped with Errors::fatal_error. This usually means the option's setter is missing from initialize_control_ints.

Parameters:

  • var_name Name of the option the control integer belongs to (for the error message).
  • control_int Control integer to check.

Returns:

The control integer, unchanged.

docs.title: function initialize_control_ints
docs.text:
void Options::Options::initialize_control_ints ()

Sets every control integer to match its string option.

Control integers are integer versions of string options that are faster to check in the code than comparing strings. The logic that assigns each one lives in the option's setter, so this calls every such setter with the option's current value. Any new option with a control integer must have its setter called here too. Otherwise its control integer stays at -1, which get_control_int reports as an error.

docs.title: Detailed Description
docs.text:
Prints a progress message each time another 1 / num_prints of the particles has been finished.

Set up with the total number of particles and print_interval, then call update with the number left as the main loop runs. With num_prints = 10, a message is printed when 90%, 80%, ..., 0% of the particles are left.

docs.title: function compact_dead_slots
docs.text:
void Slots::compact_dead_slots (
    const int *__restrict__ state,
    int *__restrict__ dead_indices,
    int *__restrict__ num_dead,
    int N
)

Kernel that gathers the indices of every dead slot into a compact list.

This is a warp-level stream compaction. Each warp votes on which of its lanes hold a dead slot (__ballot_sync), lane 0 reserves room for that many indices in dead_indices with a single atomicAdd on num_dead, and each dead lane then writes its slot index at its offset within the warp's reserved block. Using one atomic per warp instead of one per thread keeps contention low. The order of the indices between warps is not deterministic.

Parameters:

  • state State of each slot, where 0 is alive and anything else is dead.
  • dead_indices Output list of dead slot indices. Must be able to hold N indices.
  • num_dead Device counter of dead slots. Must be zeroed before the launch. Holds the number of dead slots afterward.
  • N Number of slots.

void Slots::fill_slots_cpu (
    Slots & slots,
    int & rem_parts,
    int & alive_slots,
    const Background::Background & bkg,
    const Options::Options & opts,
    std::vector< pcg32 > & rngs
)

Replaces dead particles with new ones, as long as there are particles remaining to be followed.

The dead slots are counted first. The number refilled is the smaller of the dead count and rem_parts, and rem_parts is reduced by that number. Each refilled slot gets a new particle from make_new_particle, using the random number generator of the thread doing the work, with its particle time reset to 0 and its state set to alive.

Parameters:

  • slots Particle slots to refill.
  • rem_parts Number of particles still to be followed. Reduced by the number of particles created, and never goes below 0.
  • alive_slots Set to the number of alive slots after refilling.
  • bkg Background plasma.
  • opts Simulation options.
  • rngs Random number generators, one per OpenMP thread.

docs.title: function fill_slots_gpu

void Slots::fill_slots_gpu (
    SlotsDevice & slots_d,
    int & rem_parts,
    int & alive_slots,
    pcg32 * rngs_d,
    Options::OptionsDevice * opts_d,
    const Background::BackgroundDevice & bkg_d
)

Replaces dead particles with new ones, as long as there are particles left to launch.

Runs compact_dead_slots to gather the dead slot indices, copies the number of dead slots back to the host (which waits for the kernel to finish), and then launches fill_slots_kernel with one thread per dead slot. Both use blocks of 256 threads. The fill kernel launch is asynchronous, except in DEBUG builds, where it waits for the kernel to finish and prints any error. The number of filled slots is min(rem_parts, num_dead), so the counts are updated on the host without waiting for it.

Parameters:

  • slots_d Particle slots on the device.
  • rem_parts Number of particles left to launch. Decreased by the number of slots filled.
  • alive_slots Number of alive slots after filling.
  • rngs_d Random number generators on the device.
  • opts_d Simulation options on the device.
  • bkg_d Background plasma on the device.

void Slots::fill_slots_kernel (
    SlotsDevice slots_d,
    Background::BackgroundDevice bkg_d,
    int rem_parts,
    pcg32 * rngs_d,
    const Options::OptionsDevice * opts_d
)

Kernel that fills dead slots with new particles.

One thread handles one entry of the dead slot list from compact_dead_slots, so only the first min(num_dead, rem_parts) dead slots are filled. Each creates a new particle with make_new_particle_cuda and writes it into the slot, marking it alive. The cell indices are set to 0 here and assigned afterward by find_containing_cell_gpu.

slots_d is passed by value each time since the copy time is much less than the kernel launch time, and it makes for clearer code.

  • slots_d Particle slots on the device. The dead slots are overwritten in place.
  • bkg_d Background plasma on the device.
  • rem_parts Number of particles left to launch.
  • rngs_d Random number generators on the device.
  • opts_d Simulation options on the device.

docs.title: function get_birth_vXYZ
docs.text:
Vec3d Slots::get_birth_vXYZ (
    const Background::BackgroundDevice bkg_d,
    const double t,
    const double x,
    const double y,
    const double z,
    const int tidx,
    const int xidx,
    const int yidx,
    const int zidx,
    pcg32 & rng,
    const Options::OptionsDevice * opts_d
)

Picks the starting Cartesian velocity of a new particle.

For the test backgrounds (bkg_source = "test") the velocity is fixed by the test case: 10,000 m/s in Y for the gyrate, ExB, grad-B and polarization tests, 30,000 m/s along the field line (in the X-Y plane, at angle z) for the curvature test, and at rest for the friction test.

Otherwise each component is sampled from a Maxwellian with zero mean and sigma = sqrt(kT/m), giving an isotropic velocity distribution. The temperature is imp_temp_start_val if imp_temp_start_opt is "single_value", or the main ion temperature interpolated (trilinear in space, linear in time) at the particle location if it is "main_ion". The interpolated ion temperature is held at or above min_ti, since it can go negative near the grid edges.

Parameters:

  • bkg_d Background plasma on the device, used for the ion temperature.
  • t Starting time of the particle (s).
  • x Starting computational x coordinate.
  • y Starting computational y coordinate.
  • z Starting computational z coordinate. In the curvature test, z is the toroidal angle.
  • tidx Index of the nearest background time frame.
  • xidx x index of the grid cell containing the particle.
  • yidx y index of the grid cell containing the particle.
  • zidx z index of the grid cell containing the particle.
  • rng Random number generator for this thread.
  • opts_d Simulation options on the device.

Returns:

Starting velocity {vX, vY, vZ} in Cartesian space (m/s).

The time index and grid cell indices are then found, the same as in impurity_transport.cpp, and the Cartesian velocity comes from get_birth_vXYZ. docs.title: function to_device
docs.text:
SlotsDevice Slots::Slots::to_device (
    int device_id=0
)

Allocates GPU memory for the particles and copies them to the device.

I think this should probably be moved to slots.cu...

The per-particle arrays are allocated and copied, except iters, which are not stored on the device. The work arrays used by the GPU kernels (all_dead, num_dead and dead_indices) are also allocated, and all_dead is initialized to false. If GPU support was not compiled in, an error is printed and an empty SlotsDevice is returned.

Parameters:

  • device_id ID of the GPU to allocate the memory on.

Returns:

SlotsDevice struct holding the device pointers. The memory must be released with free_slots.

docs.title: function to_host
docs.text:
Slots Slots::Slots::to_host (
    const SlotsDevice & slots_d
)

Copies the particles from the device back into a new host Slots object.

The mass and the per-particle arrays on the device are copied back. iters and the atomic number are not stored on the device, so they are left at zero in the returned object. The device memory is not freed, use free_slots for that. If GPU support was not compiled in, only N and the mass are set.

Parameters:

  • slots_d SlotsDevice struct returned by to_device.

Returns:

Host Slots object holding a copy of the device data.

docs.title: Detailed Description
docs.text:
Device-side copy of a Slots object, made by Slots::to_device and freed with free_slots.

A plain struct of device pointers, so it can be passed to kernels by value. Each per-particle array has N entries, one per slot, and slot i is handled by thread i in the kernels. Positions and their velocities (x, vx) are in computational coordinates, and vX, vY, vZ are the Cartesian velocity.

docs.title: function read_test
docs.text:
Background::Background Test::read_test (
    const Options::Options & opts
)

Creates the hardcoded test background chosen by the test_opt option.

Every case uses the same grid: 128 time frames from 0 to 50 us, and 32 x 32 x 9 cells in x, y and z. The plasma is uniform, with ne = 1e20 m^-3 and Te = Ti = 1 eV. The cases are:

  • gyrate (0): slab, B_Z = 1 T, no electric field. The particle just gyrates.
  • exb (1): slab, B_Z = 1 T and E_Y = 500 V/m, for an ExB drift.
  • gradb (2): slab, B_Z = 1 + 5 y T (a 5 T/m gradient in y), no electric field, for a grad-B drift.
  • polarization (3): slab, B_Z = 1 T and E_Y = 5000 - 1e7 t V/m (falling by 10 V/us), for a polarization drift.
  • curvature (4): cylindrical (x = R, y = Z, z = phi), a purely toroidal B = 10 T, no electric field, for a curvature drift.
  • friction_force (5): slab, B_X = 1 T and a background flow of u_X = 1000 m/s, no electric field, to show the friction force from the collision model.

The slab is 5 x 5 x 3 cm, x from 0 to 0.05 m, y from -0.025 to 0.025 m and z from -0.015 to 0.015 m, with x = X, y = Y and z = Z. The cylindrical volume has R from 2.00 to 2.05 m, Z from -0.025 to 0.025 m and phi from 0 to about pi/2. Only the background flow is nonzero in the friction force case. The reciprocal basis vectors and Jacobian are set for each geometry. The tangent basis vectors are not set.

Parameters:

  • opts Simulation options, used for test_opt.

Returns:

Background holding the test plasma.

void Timer::Timer::print_summary () const

Prints a summary of the time spent in each section to stdout.

Each row shows the section name, indented to show which sections are part of another, followed by its total time, its number of calls and the average time per call. The times are lined up in a column.

docs.title: function bilinear_interp
docs.text:
template<typename T>
inline T Utilities::bilinear_interp (
    const T *__restrict__ table,
    const T *__restrict__ x_grid,
    int nx,
    const T *__restrict__ y_grid,
    int ny,
    T x,
    T y
)

Performs bilinear interpolation on a flattened two-dimensional lookup table stored in device memory.

The function locates the grid cell that contains the point (x, y) with a linear search, computes the interpolation weights in each dimension, and returns the bilinearly interpolated value. Interpolation weights are clamped to the range [0, 1] to prevent extrapolation beyond the boundaries of the tabulated data. nx and ny must both be at least 2.

The table is assumed to be stored in row-major order with dimensions nx × ny, where the flattened index corresponding to (ix, iy) is ix * ny + iy.

Template parameters:

  • T Floating-point data type used for the table and coordinate arrays.

Parameters:

  • table Flattened two-dimensional lookup table of size nx * ny.
  • x_grid Monotonically increasing x-coordinate array of length nx.
  • nx Number of x-grid points.
  • y_grid Monotonically increasing y-coordinate array of length ny.
  • ny Number of y-grid points.
  • x X-coordinate at which to evaluate the table.
  • y Y-coordinate at which to evaluate the table.

Returns:

Bilinearly interpolated value at (x, y).

    const double x0,
    const double y0,
    const double x1,

    const double z00,
    const double z10,
    const double z01,
    const double z11,
    const double x,
    const double y
)

Performs bilinear interpolation within a rectangular region in two-dimensional (x, y) space.

The rectangle is defined by the coordinates (x0, y0) and (x1, y1), with values specified at each of the four corners. Interpolation is performed first along the x direction and then along the y direction to obtain the value at (x, y).

Corner indexing follows the usual convention:

z00 : (x0, y0) z10 : (x1, y0) z01 : (x0, y1) z11 : (x1, y1)

Parameters:

  • x0 Lower x-coordinate of the rectangle.
  • y0 Lower y-coordinate of the rectangle.
  • x1 Upper x-coordinate of the rectangle.
  • y1 Upper y-coordinate of the rectangle.
  • z00 Value at (x0, y0).
  • z10 Value at (x1, y0).
  • z01 Value at (x0, y1).
  • z11 Value at (x1, y1).
  • x X-coordinate at which to evaluate the interpolated value.
  • y Y-coordinate at which to evaluate the interpolated value.

Returns:

Bilinearly interpolated value at (x, y).

docs.text:
std::pair< int, int > Utilities::bracket_indices (
    const std::vector< double > & x,
    double x0
)

Finds the indices of the two grid points that bracket a specified coordinate value.

For values within the coordinate range, the returned indices correspond to the nearest lower and upper grid points that surround x0. For values outside the coordinate range, the first or last valid interval is returned so that interpolation can proceed without accessing elements beyond the array bounds.

The input coordinate array is assumed to be sorted in ascending order.

Parameters:

  • x Sorted coordinate array.
  • x0 Coordinate value for which bracketing indices are sought.

Returns:

Pair containing the lower and upper bracketing indices {lo, hi}.

docs.title: function get_neighbor_index
docs.text:
template<typename T>
int Utilities::get_neighbor_index (
    const double val,
    const std::vector< T > & cell_centers,
    const int idx
)

Returns the index of the nearest neighboring cell center to a specified cell center index.

The neighbor is selected based on which side of the cell center the value lies. If the value is greater than the cell center, the neighboring index to the right is returned. If the value is less than or equal to the cell center, the neighboring index to the left is returned.

At the edges of the grid, where only one neighboring cell exists, that neighbor is returned regardless of which side of the cell center the value lies on.

Template parameters:

  • T Data type of the cell center coordinates.

Parameters:

  • val Coordinate value of interest.
  • cell_centers Array of cell center coordinates.
  • idx Index of the reference cell center.

Returns:

Index of the neighboring cell center closest to the side of the cell containing val.

docs.title: function get_neighbor_index_cuda
docs.text:
inline int Utilities::get_neighbor_index_cuda (
    const double val,
    const double * cell_centers,
    int idx,
    int N
)

Finds the index of the neighboring cell center on val's side of the center of cell idx.

This picks the second point to interpolate between. If val is above cell_centers[idx], the neighbor is idx + 1, otherwise (including val exactly at the center) it's idx - 1. At the first or last cell, the only neighbor is returned regardless of side, and the clamped interpolation weights then hold the value constant past the outer cell centers. Same logic as the CPU version, Utilities:: get_neighbor_index, written without branches.

N must be at least 2. With N = 1 there is no neighbor and the returned index is out of range.

Parameters:

  • val Coordinate of the point.
  • cell_centers Cell center coordinates, length N.
  • idx Index of the cell containing val.
  • N Number of cells.

Returns:

Index of the neighboring cell.

template<typename T, std::size_t N>
T Utilities::linear_interpolate (
    const std::array< T, N > & xarr,
    const std::array< T, N > & yarr,
    T x
)

Linearly interpolates a fixed-size table at x.

Searches the table from the start for the interval containing x, so xarr can be increasing or decreasing. For a large, evenly spaced table, linear_interpolate_uniform is much faster.

This is defined in the header file here because otherwise we would need to have definitions in the source file for every N that we use (which is of course silly and not a real option).

Template parameters:

  • T Floating-point type of the table.
  • N Length of the table, deduced from the arrays.

Parameters:

  • xarr Table x values.
  • yarr Table y values.
  • x Point to interpolate at.

Returns:

Interpolated y value.

Exception:

  • std::out_of_range If x is outside the range of xarr.

Broadcasts a vector from a root MPI rank to all other ranks in the communicator.

The root rank provides the vector contents and size. The vector size is first broadcast to all ranks, allowing non-root ranks to resize their local vectors before the vector data itself is broadcast.

The element type T must have a corresponding MPI datatype defined through mpi_type<T>::type.

Splits a string into whitespace-delimited tokens.

Consecutive whitespace characters are treated as a single delimiter, and leading or trailing whitespace is ignored. The resulting vector contains each extracted token in the order it appears in the input string.

Internally, the string is parsed using a std::istringstream and repeated applications of the stream extraction operator.

Parameters:

Returns:

Vector containing the whitespace-delimited tokens extracted from the input string.

inline double Utilities::trilinear_interpolate (
    const double x0,
    const double y0,
    const double z0,
    const double x1,
    const double y1,
    const double z1,
    const double v000,
    const double v100,

    const double v001,
    const double v101,
    const double v011,
    const double v111,
    const double x,
    const double y,
    const double z
)

Performs trilinear interpolation within a rectangular cell in (x, y, z) space.

The cell is defined by the coordinates (x0, y0, z0) and (x1, y1, z1), with values specified at each of the eight cell corners. Interpolation weights are clamped to the range [0, 1] to prevent extrapolation beyond the cell boundaries. As a result, points outside the cell return the value on the nearest cell face, edge, or corner.

Corner indexing follows the usual convention:

v000 : (x0, y0, z0) v100 : (x1, y0, z0) v010 : (x0, y1, z0) v110 : (x1, y1, z0) v001 : (x0, y0, z1) v101 : (x1, y0, z1) v011 : (x0, y1, z1) v111 : (x1, y1, z1)

Parameters:

  • x0 Lower x-coordinate of the cell.
  • y0 Lower y-coordinate of the cell.
  • z0 Lower z-coordinate of the cell.
  • x1 Upper x-coordinate of the cell.
  • y1 Upper y-coordinate of the cell.
  • z1 Upper z-coordinate of the cell.
  • v000 Field value at (x0, y0, z0).
  • v100 Field value at (x1, y0, z0).
  • v010 Field value at (x0, y1, z0).
  • v110 Field value at (x1, y1, z0).
  • v001 Field value at (x0, y0, z1).
  • v101 Field value at (x1, y0, z1).
  • v011 Field value at (x0, y1, z1).
  • v111 Field value at (x1, y1, z1).
  • x X-coordinate at which to evaluate the field.
  • y Y-coordinate at which to evaluate the field.
  • z Z-coordinate at which to evaluate the field.

Returns:

Interpolated field value.

Trilinearly interpolates between the 8 corners of a box at (x, y, z).

The box has one corner at (x0, y0, z0) and the opposite one at (x0 + dx, y0 + dy, z0 + dz). dx, dy and dz can be negative, so x0 doesn't have to be the low corner. Corner values are named by offset, e.g., v100 is at (x0 + dx, y0, z0). The weights are clamped to [0, 1], so points outside the box get the value on the nearest face instead of being extrapolated.

Parameters:

  • x0 x coordinate of the origin corner.
  • y0 y coordinate of the origin corner.
  • z0 z coordinate of the origin corner.
  • dx Box size in x. Must not be 0.
  • dy Box size in y. Must not be 0.
  • dz Box size in z. Must not be 0.
  • v000 Value at (x0, y0, z0).
  • v100 Value at (x0 + dx, y0, z0).
  • v010 Value at (x0, y0 + dy, z0).
  • v110 Value at (x0 + dx, y0 + dy, z0).
  • v001 Value at (x0, y0, z0 + dz).
  • v101 Value at (x0 + dx, y0, z0 + dz).
  • v011 Value at (x0, y0 + dy, z0 + dz).
  • v111 Value at (x0 + dx, y0 + dy, z0 + dz).
  • x x coordinate of the point.
  • y y coordinate of the point.
  • z z coordinate of the point.

Returns:

Interpolated value at (x, y, z).

docs.title: Detailed Description
docs.text:
3D array of values, stored as a flattened 1D vector.

A value is accessed with the parentheses operator, e.g., vec(i, j, k). The data is stored in row-major order (k varies fastest), so it can be copied straight to and from GPU arrays. See vectors.cpp for the member function docs.

Artificial constructor that should never be called.

docs.title: function next_double
docs.text:
inline double pcg32::next_double ()

Returns the next random double in [0, 1).

Uses two calls to next_uint to fill all 53 bits of a double's mantissa, so the result is a multiple of 2^-53 (about 1e-16). With fewer bits, comparisons like r < p would be wrong for small p, since every p smaller than the spacing would act the same.

Returns:

Uniformly distributed value in [0, 1).

docs.title: function normal
docs.text:
inline double pcg32::normal (
    double mean,
    double stddev
)

Returns a normally distributed random number.

Uses the Box-Muller transform, which makes two independent normal values from two uniform ones. The second is cached in spare and returned by the next call, so only every other call draws new uniform numbers. The cached value is in standard units, so the next call can use a different mean and stddev.

Parameters:

  • mean Mean of the distribution.
  • stddev Standard deviation of the distribution.

Returns:

Random value from the normal distribution.

pcg32 * init_rngs_cuda (
    Slots::SlotsDevice & slots_d,
    uint64_t base_seed
)

Allocates and initializes the random number generators for the slots on a GPU.

Launches init_rngs_kernel with blocks of 256 threads, so the array is rounded up to a whole number of blocks and has at least slots_d.N generators. Generator i belongs to slot i. Waits for the kernel to finish before returning. The array is allocated on the current device, so that must be the GPU slots_d is on.

Parameters:

  • slots_d Particle slots on the device, used for the number of slots.
  • base_seed Base seed for the generators. See init_rngs_kernel.

Returns:

Device pointer to the array of generators. The caller owns it and must free it with free_rngs.

The background fields are defined at the grid cell centers (and, for 4D fields, at each time frame). To interpolate at a particle, a stencil is first built with build_stencil_3d or build_stencil_4d. It holds the indices of the 8 cell centers that bound the particle and the geometry of the box they form. Everything is inline so it can be used in any kernel.

docs.title: function flan
docs.text:
void flan (
    const Inputs & inpts
)

Runs a Flan simulation with the given input options.

The steps are:

  • Load the options from inpts, filling in defaults for any not given (Options::load_options).
  • Read the background plasma on rank 0 (Background::read_bkg) and broadcast it to every rank.
  • Follow the impurities on every rank (ImpurityTransport::follow_impurities).
  • Combine the statistics from every rank onto rank 0 (Impurity::reduce_stats), and calculate the density, velocities, charge and Nanbu s from them.
  • Save the results on rank 0 (SaveResults::save_results) and print the timing summary.

MPI must already be initialized when flan is called, and the caller finalizes it afterwards. Every rank must call flan.

Parameters:

  • inpts Input options from the input file. Options not in inpts keep their default values.

docs.text: PCG32 (the XSH RR variant of M. E. O'Neill's PCG family) has 64 bits of state and returns 32-bit numbers. It's small, fast and doesn't use the standard library, so the same generator works on both the host and the device. docs.title: Detailed Description
docs.text:
The background's time and coordinate arrays are small and read by nearly every kernel, so they are kept in constant memory, which is cached and faster to read than global memory when the threads in a warp read the same address. Background::to_device fills them with cudaMemcpyToSymbol. Constant memory is per GPU, and to_device selects the GPU before copying, so each GPU gets its own copy.

The arrays have a fixed size of MAX_1D (see device_constants.cuh). Only the first tdim, xdim, ydim or zdim elements (dim + 1 for the grid edges) are set; the rest are unused.

These are compiled with relocatable device code, so there is one copy of each variable per executable. Code that needs them must be linked with the same copy that Background::to_device fills in (see tests/CMakeLists.txt).

docs.title: function init_rngs_cuda
docs.text:
pcg32 * init_rngs_cuda (
    Slots::SlotsDevice & slots_d,
    uint64_t base_seed
)

Allocates and initializes the random number generators for the slots on a GPU.

Launches init_rngs_kernel with blocks of 256 threads, so the array is rounded up to a whole number of blocks and has at least slots_d.N generators. Generator i belongs to slot i. Waits for the kernel to finish before returning. The array is allocated on the current device, so that must be the GPU slots_d is on.

Parameters:

  • slots_d Particle slots on the device, used for the number of slots.
  • base_seed Base seed for the generators. See init_rngs_kernel.

Returns:

Device pointer to the array of generators. The caller owns it and must free it with free_rngs.

docs.title: function flan
docs.text:
void flan (
    const Inputs & inpts
)

Runs a Flan simulation with the given input options.

The steps are:

  • Load the options from inpts, filling in defaults for any not given (Options::load_options).
  • Read the background plasma on rank 0 (Background::read_bkg) and broadcast it to every rank.
  • Follow the impurities on every rank (ImpurityTransport::follow_impurities).
  • Combine the statistics from every rank onto rank 0 (Impurity::reduce_stats), and calculate the density, velocities, charge and Nanbu s from them.
  • Save the results on rank 0 (SaveResults::save_results) and print the timing summary.

MPI must already be initialized when flan is called, and the caller finalizes it afterwards. Every rank must call flan.

Parameters:

  • inpts Input options from the input file. Options not in inpts keep their default values.

docs.title: Namespaces
docs.text: Type Name namespace SaveResults

docs.title: Detailed Description
docs.text:
Right now only outputting everything into a single netCDF file is supported. Important to know that NcFile inherits from NcGroup, so we can pass an NcFile object into a function that calls for an NcGroup.

The file is named <case_name>.nc and has four groups: input (the options used), geometry (grids, metric coefficients and basis vectors), background (the plasma) and output (the impurity results). The 4D arrays have dimensions (time, x, y, z), and the grid edge arrays use the "grid x", "grid y" and "grid z" dimensions, one longer than x, y and z. Every variable has a description attribute, and numeric ones a units attribute. Units of "(?)" depend on the computational coordinates used.

docs.text: Type Name namespace Slots

docs.title: Detailed Description
docs.text:
A Slots object holds a fixed number of particle "slots". Each slot holds one particle that is followed until it dies, at which point the slot is refilled with a new particle by fill_slots_cpu (or its CUDA version) until the requested number of particles has been followed. The reason for this layout is to enable a structure of arrays (SoA) memeory layout, which is more efficient memory-wise.

docs.title: Namespaces
docs.text: Type Name namespace Vectors

docs.title: Detailed Description
docs.text:
This file contains some simple implementations of multidimensional vectors. Instead of storing them as actual multidimensional vectors, they are stored as flattened vectors and then () is overloaded to act as indexing. The last index varies fastest (row-major order), the same as the flattened arrays used on the GPU (see calc_3d_index_cuda and calc_4d_index_cuda).

The bottom of this file includes instantiations of Vector3D and Vector4D for the different types needed (e.g., int, double, ...). This is a peculiarity needed when splitting the declarations and definitions between a header and source file, needed so the linker can find the classes for each template type.
